name: Hungary
blurb: From St Stephen's crown to Hungary's prime ministers today
dateConvention: Dates are Julian until Hungary switched to the Gregorian calendar in 1587. Reigns start at a coronation or election as noted; after Mohács (1526) rival kings and the Ottomans split the country. From 1918 the deck follows whoever held real power, and from 1990 it follows the prime ministers.

reigns.tagline: The raider's grandson who made Hungary a kingdom
reigns.cameToPower: Crowned with a crown from Rome
reigns.previously: The Magyars ride in around 895, raid Europe, and lose at Lechfeld 955.
paragraphs: Around 895 Árpád led the Magyar tribes over the Carpathians into the plain of the Danube. For sixty years their horsemen raided half of Europe, until the Germans crushed them at the Lechfeld in 955. Árpád's great-grandson Géza saw the way the wind blew. He let in missionaries and had his son baptised. The boy was born Vajk. He grew up as Stephen.

When Géza died in 997, his kinsman Koppány claimed the lead by old pagan custom. Stephen beat him in battle and had the body cut into four pieces and nailed up in four towns. Then he got himself crowned king, at Christmas 1000 or on 1 January 1001 (sources differ), with a crown sent by Pope Sylvester II. He married Gisela of Bavaria, set up bishoprics and counties, and made his people pay tithes and build churches.

His only grown son, Emeric, was killed by a wild boar while hunting in 1031. The obvious heir was Stephen's cousin Vazul, a man with a pagan streak. Vazul was blinded and his sons fled abroad. Stephen died on 15 August 1038 and was made a saint in 1083. His right hand, the Holy Right, still goes on parade through Budapest every 20 August.

claims.text: Pope Sylvester II sent Stephen his crown.
claims.note: Bishop Hartvic's Life of Stephen (c. 1100) says so; Thietmar of Merseburg credits Emperor Otto III's favour. The Holy Crown that survives today was made later.

claims.text: Koppány's body was quartered and displayed on town gates.
claims.note: Told in Stephen's medieval Lives and the chronicles; one part went to Gyulafehérvár in Transylvania as a warning.

claims.text: Stephen ordered Vazul blinded and molten lead poured into his ears.
claims.note: The chronicles disagree on who gave the order; some blame Queen Gisela. The lead detail comes from the 14th-century chronicle.

reigns.hook: The saint-king leaves no son. The crown goes to his sister's boy, Peter Orseolo, half Venetian and wholly unloved. Out in the countryside, the old gods are not quite dead.

reigns.tagline: Stephen's Venetian nephew, and nobody's idea of a king
reigns.cameToPower: Named heir by his uncle Stephen
reigns.previously: Stephen dies with no son, and his chosen heir is a Venetian nephew.
paragraphs: Peter was born in Venice in 1011, the son of Doge Otto Orseolo and one of King Stephen's sisters. When his father was thrown out of Venice in 1026, Peter landed at his uncle's court. Stephen's own son was dead and his cousin Vazul had been blinded, so the old king picked his Venetian nephew as heir. Plenty of Hungarians never forgave him for it.

Peter took over in August 1038 and made enemies fast. He filled the court with Germans and Italians and handed them the best jobs. He fell out with Stephen's widow, Queen Gisela, took her lands and kept her under watch. The chronicle calls him proud and cruel. In 1041 the nobles had had enough and threw him out. He fled west and ended up at the court of the German king, Henry III, asking for an army.

claims.text: Peter robbed Stephen's widow Gisela and kept her a virtual prisoner.
claims.note: The Hungarian chronicles say so, and they hated Peter. Gisela did later leave Hungary and died as abbess of a convent in Passau.

claims.text: Stephen himself chose Peter as his heir.
claims.note: The Hungarian chronicles say Stephen named his sister's son after Emeric's death, and historians generally accept it.

reigns.hook: Peter is gone. The nobles pick one of their own: Samuel Aba, the palatine, who married into Stephen's family. But Peter is at the German court, and the German king is listening.

reigns.tagline: The home-grown king who took on the German Empire
reigns.cameToPower: Elected after Peter was thrown out
reigns.previously: The nobles throw out King Peter, who runs to the German king.
paragraphs: Samuel Aba was a big man in Stephen's kingdom. His family held lands around the Mátra hills, he had served as palatine, the top officer of the realm, and he was married to one of Stephen's sisters. When the nobles chased Peter out in 1041, he was the obvious pick, a Hungarian with a royal wife and no foreign hangers-on.

Aba did not sit still. His men raided Austria and Bavaria, which only drew the Germans down on him. At home he grew suspicious. When he found a plot among his own councillors, he had a number of them put to death without trial during Lent. The chronicle says he sided with the common people against the lords. At Easter, Bishop Gerard of Csanád refused to set the crown on his head because of the killings.

Henry III marched in with Peter in 1044. On 5 July the armies met at Ménfő, near Győr, and Aba's army broke. He fled east and was caught and killed. He was buried in a nearby church, says the chronicle, and later moved to his family's monastery at Abasár.

claims.text: Aba had about fifty plotting nobles put to death.
claims.note: The number comes from the 14th-century chronicle tradition, long after the event; no contemporary source counts them.

claims.text: Aba was killed by Hungarians as he fled from Ménfő.
claims.note: The Hungarian chronicles say so. Some German annals say he was captured and executed on Peter's orders.

claims.text: Aba's wife was a sister of King Stephen.
claims.note: The chronicles make him Stephen's brother-in-law, but historians still argue over exactly how his wife was related to Stephen.

reigns.hook: Aba is dead. Peter rides back behind the German army, and this time he will pay any price to keep the crown.

reigns.title: Peter, Again
reigns.tagline: Back on German spears, out in a pagan storm
reigns.cameToPower: Put back by Henry III's army
reigns.previously: Samuel Aba is routed at Ménfő and killed as he flees.
paragraphs: Peter was back, and he knew whose army had done it. At Whitsun 1045, in Stephen's church at Székesfehérvár, he handed Henry III a gilded lance and took Hungary back from him as a fief. Stephen had made a kingdom answerable to nobody. His nephew had just made it a German possession.

That was too much. In 1046 the lords invited Vazul's sons Andrew and Levente home from exile, and a pagan rising led by a man named Vata swept the country. Priests were murdered and churches burned. On 24 September the Venetian monk Gerard, Bishop of Csanád, who had once taught Stephen's son, was killed in Buda. Peter ran for the western border, was cornered at Zámoly, and was blinded. He is said to have died soon after.

claims.text: Peter handed Hungary to Henry III as a fief in 1045.
claims.note: German writers such as Hermann of Reichenau and the Hungarian chronicles both describe the Whitsun ceremony at Székesfehérvár.

claims.text: Bishop Gerard was rolled down the hill in a cart, or a barrel, and finished off below.
claims.note: His death in 1046 is certain. The cart comes from his later Lives; the spiked barrel is a later embroidery. The hill in Buda is named after him.

claims.text: Peter died soon after he was blinded.
claims.note: The chronicles say so, but some historians read German evidence as showing he lived on, perhaps until about 1059.

reigns.hook: Peter is blind and the pagans are loose. The new king is Vazul's son Andrew, home from Kiev, and he has to tame the very rising that brought him to power.

reigns.tagline: The pagans' pick who sided with the Church
reigns.cameToPower: Rode home on a pagan revolt
reigns.reignEnded: Beaten by Béla, died of wounds
reigns.previously: Pagan rebels catch King Peter and blind him.
paragraphs: Andrew was a son of Vazul, the cousin Stephen had blinded. He spent years in exile and ended up in Kiev, where he married a daughter of Grand Prince Yaroslav the Wise. In 1046 the pagan rebels brought him home and expected the old gods back. Once crowned, he did the opposite: he ordered everyone back to the Christian faith on pain of death. In 1055 he founded Tihany Abbey on Lake Balaton, where he is buried.

Henry III, now emperor, wanted his fief back. He invaded in 1051, and the Hungarians burned the land ahead of him until his hungry army turned for home. In 1052 he besieged Pressburg (now Bratislava) and failed again. The chronicle gives the credit to a diver named Zotmund, who swam out at night and holed the German supply boats.

Andrew had called his brother Béla home and given him a third of the kingdom. Then he had his small son Solomon crowned in 1057. At Várkony, says the chronicle, he set a crown and a sword before Béla and made him choose. Béla took the sword and fled to Poland. He came back with a Polish army in 1060 and beat Andrew, who died of his injuries at Zirc.

claims.text: At Várkony, King Andrew made Béla choose between a crown and a sword.
claims.note: The 14th-century chronicle tells it: the sword meant keeping his duchy, the crown meant treason and death.

claims.text: A diver named Zotmund sank the emperor's boats at Pressburg.
claims.note: Only the Hungarian chronicles name him. German sources confirm the siege failed but say nothing of a diver.

claims.text: Tihany Abbey's founding charter is the oldest original document with Hungarian words in it.
claims.note: The 1055 charter is in Latin but names places in Hungarian; the original is kept at Pannonhalma Abbey.

reigns.hook: Andrew is dead. His brother Béla, the man who chose the sword and took the crown anyway, is king at last. Andrew's boy Solomon has fled to the Germans.

reigns.tagline: Three short years, a new coin and a falling throne
reigns.reignEnded: Crushed when his throne gave way
reigns.previously: Andrew I is beaten by his brother Béla and dies of his wounds.
paragraphs: Béla had waited a long time for this. He was crowned at Székesfehérvár on 6 December 1060, while his nephew Solomon sheltered in Germany, engaged to the little sister of the boy king Henry IV. Béla knew the Germans would come for him sooner or later, so he moved fast.

He struck a new silver coinage, fixed prices, and moved weekly markets from Sunday to Saturday. In 1061 he called two elders from every village to an assembly at Székesfehérvár. A crowd turned up demanding the old pagan ways back. Béla asked for three days to think, quietly brought in troops, and crushed them. It was the last pagan rising Hungary ever saw.

In 1063 a German army set off to put Solomon back on the throne. At his manor at Dömös, says the chronicle, Béla's throne broke under him and he was badly hurt. He died by the Kanizsva stream on 11 September, and his sons stepped aside to let Solomon in.

claims.text: Béla I died after his throne collapsed under him at Dömös.
claims.note: This is the chronicle's story. Some historians suspect foul play, but there is no evidence either way.

claims.text: Béla moved weekly markets from Sunday to Saturday.
claims.note: Only the chronicles credit Béla. Place names like Szombathely, 'Saturday market', show such markets were common, not who started them.

claims.text: Béla crushed the last pagan rising in Hungary in 1061.
claims.note: The chronicle describes the assembly in detail, and no later pagan revolt is recorded.

reigns.hook: Béla is dead, and a German army is at the border. The Hungarians let the boy Solomon back in. Béla's sons Géza and Ladislaus step aside, for now.

reigns.tagline: The boy king who lost his throne to his cousins

start.note: restored by German troops after Béla I died

reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of Andrew I; Béla I's nephew
reigns.cameToPower: Brought back by a German army
reigns.reignEnded: Beaten by his cousins at Mogyoród
reigns.previously: Béla I dies after his throne collapses at Dömös.
paragraphs: Solomon was about ten when German troops brought him home in 1063. His bride Judith was the sister of the young German king Henry IV. His cousins Géza and Ladislaus, Béla's sons, had fled to Poland, but in 1064 the bishops brokered a deal. The cousins got their father's duchy, a third of the kingdom, and at Easter in Pécs, Géza himself set the crown on Solomon's head.

For a while the three made a fine team. In 1068 they beat raiders at Cserhalom, where young Ladislaus chased down a warrior who had carried off a girl. In 1071 they took Belgrade from the Byzantines. But the Byzantine commander surrendered to Géza, not to the king, and the quarrel over the loot turned into a quarrel over who really ruled.

By 1074 it was war. Solomon won the first round, but on 14 March Géza and Ladislaus beat him at Mogyoród, north-east of Pest. Solomon fled to Pressburg on the western border, held it with German help, and went on calling himself king.

claims.text: At Cserhalom, Ladislaus rescued a girl from a warrior who had carried her off.
claims.note: The chronicles and Ladislaus's legend tell it (they call the place Kerlés); it became a favourite church mural.

claims.text: Géza crowned Solomon himself at Pécs in 1064.
claims.note: The chronicle describes the Easter ceremony, part of the peace deal between the cousins.

reigns.hook: Géza is master of Hungary, but Solomon still holds Pressburg and still has a crown on his head. Géza needs a crown of his own, and it comes from Constantinople.

reigns.tagline: The king whose crown came from Constantinople
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of Béla I; Solomon's cousin
reigns.previously: Solomon loses at Mogyoród but holds on to Pressburg.
paragraphs: Géza was Béla I's eldest son, a careful man who had spent years as Solomon's partner and rival. After Mogyoród he was king in all but crown. He got one from Byzantium: Emperor Michael VII Doukas sent him a gold crown with enamel pictures, one of them showing Géza himself. That crown is now the lower band of the Holy Crown of Hungary.

The chronicle says Géza and Ladislaus had vowed a church if they won, and at Vác a stag with candles burning on its antlers showed them where to build it. Géza felt uneasy all the same. Solomon had been crowned first, and Géza talked of handing back the throne if he could keep his duchy. Nothing came of it.
He died on 25 April 1077. His sons Coloman and Álmos were still boys, so the lords passed them over and chose his brother Ladislaus.

claims.text: The lower band of the Holy Crown was a gift to Géza from Emperor Michael VII.
claims.note: Its enamel plaques show Michael VII and name 'Geobitzas, faithful king of Turkia', the Byzantine name for Géza and his country.

claims.text: A stag with burning candles on its antlers showed Géza and Ladislaus where to build Vác cathedral.
claims.note: Told in the 14th-century chronicle as a sign from God; Géza did found the church at Vác.

claims.text: Géza offered to give the throne back to Solomon.
claims.note: The chronicle says so, but it was written under Géza's descendants and may be polishing his image.

reigns.hook: Géza is dead. His younger brother Ladislaus, a giant of a man and a hero of the Cuman wars, takes the crown. Solomon, the boy king crowned years ago, is still alive and still plotting.

reigns.tagline: The giant knight-king every Hungarian boy wanted to be
reigns.previously: Géza I dies. The ousted King Solomon is still alive and still crowned.
paragraphs: Ladislaus was the hero of the chronicles: tall, strong and pious, a head taller than anyone in the army. Years before he was king, he had cut down a Cuman raider at Kerlés and, says the legend, rescued the girl the man had carried off. Murals of that fight still survive in churches across old Hungary.

As king he dealt with Solomon, locked him up, let him go, and beat him again when he came back with Cuman allies. In 1083 he had Stephen, Emeric and Bishop Gerard declared saints. His laws were brutal: thieves could be hanged and their children sold into slavery. When his sister's husband, King Zvonimir of Croatia, died, Ladislaus marched in and in 1091 put his nephew Álmos in charge there.
He died on 29 July 1095, with no son. He had preferred Álmos as heir, but it was Álmos's elder brother Coloman who got the crown. Ladislaus was made a saint in 1192.

claims.text: Ladislaus rescued a girl from a Cuman warrior after the battle of Kerlés.
claims.note: The story comes from his 12th–13th-century legend and the chronicles; it became a favourite church mural, painted in dozens of churches.

claims.text: Ladislaus was about to lead the First Crusade when he died.
claims.note: Later chronicles say so. No contemporary crusade source names him as leader.

claims.text: Ladislaus wanted Álmos, not Coloman, as his heir.
claims.note: The chronicle says so, but it was written under Álmos's descendants, who had every reason to say it.

reigns.hook: The knight-king is dead. The crown goes to his nephew Coloman, a bookish man meant for the Church. His brother Álmos thinks it should have been his.

reigns.tagline: The bookworm king who said witches don't exist
reigns.cameToPower: Took the crown over his brother
reigns.previously: The knight-king Ladislaus dies, preparing for a crusade.
paragraphs: Coloman had been trained for the Church, and Hungarians remember him as Könyves, the book-lover. Within a year of his crowning the First Crusade came marching through. Coloman let the disciplined armies pass, but bands that robbed and fought their way along got a hard answer. In 1096 Count Emicho's mob besieged Moson and was routed.

He was sharp and ruthless. In 1102 he was crowned King of Croatia, and the two crowns stayed linked for over 800 years. His laws were modern for the day: one decree says there should be no trials of witches, because such witches do not exist.

His brother Álmos plotted against him again and again. Around 1113 Coloman lost patience and had Álmos and Álmos's little son Béla blinded, to make sure his own son Stephen would rule. He died on 3 February 1116.

claims.text: Coloman's law said: of witches, which do not exist, let no mention be made.
claims.note: It is in his decrees. It covers night-flying 'strigae'; ordinary sorcerers could still be punished.

claims.text: Coloman was hairy, hunchbacked, lame and half-blind.
claims.note: The 14th-century chronicle says so, but its text goes back to writers serving Álmos's line, who hated him.

claims.text: Coloman had Álmos and his son Béla blinded.
claims.note: Hungarian chronicles and outside sources agree; Béla grew up to become king anyway.

reigns.hook: Coloman's son Stephen II, still a boy, takes the crown and picks fights with every neighbour. Hidden in a monastery, the blinded boy Béla is growing up.

reigns.tagline: A teenage king at war with every neighbour
reigns.reignEnded: Died childless, in a monk's habit
reigns.previously: Coloman dies, having blinded his brother and his little nephew Béla.
paragraphs: Stephen was Coloman's son, crowned as a boy in 1116, and trouble arrived at once. Venice took back the Dalmatian towns that same year. A peace meeting with the Bohemians on the Olšava river turned into a battle, and the Hungarians were routed.

He never stopped fighting after that. He meddled in the wars of the Russian princes and quarrelled with Venice again. When the Byzantine emperor John II took in his uncle Álmos, the blinded rebel, Stephen went to war with Byzantium in 1127. His armies raided deep into the Balkans, and a peace a couple of years later left things much as they were.

Stephen had no son. The chronicle says he first picked his sister's son Saul as heir. Then it turned out that the blinded Béla, Álmos's son, was alive and hidden in a monastery. Stephen gave him estates and a Serbian bride, Helena. Stephen died on 1 March 1131, having taken a monk's habit.

claims.text: Stephen II accepted the blinded Béla as his heir.
claims.note: The chronicle says Stephen gave Béla lands and a wife, but also that he had named Saul first. Historians disagree over who really chose Béla.

claims.text: Stephen's army was routed by the Bohemians on the Olšava in 1116.
claims.note: Cosmas of Prague, writing within a decade, describes the meeting that turned into a battle.

claims.text: Stephen II died of dysentery.
claims.note: The chronicle gives the cause; there is no other account.

reigns.hook: Stephen II is dead. The crown goes to the man Coloman blinded as a child. Béla cannot see, but his wife Helena can, and she has a list of names.

reigns.tagline: The blinded boy who became king, and his queen's revenge
reigns.cameToPower: Named heir by childless Stephen II
reigns.previously: Stephen II dies childless. The blinded Béla is next in line.
paragraphs: Béla was a small boy when his uncle Coloman had him and his father blinded. Monks hid him for years. On 28 April 1131 he was crowned at Székesfehérvár, a blind king of about 22. He needed eyes, and his wife Helena of Serbia supplied them, with her brother Beloš never far away.

Helena wanted revenge. At an assembly near Arad in 1131 the nobles who had backed the blinding were seized and cut down in front of everyone, and their lands handed to Béla's men. In 1132 a pretender named Boris, who claimed to be Coloman's son, invaded with Polish help. Béla's army beat him on the Sajó river.

In 1137 Béla took the title King of Rama, a claim on Bosnia. The chronicle says he drank, and that courtiers got whatever they wanted out of him when he was drunk. He died on 13 February 1141, leaving the crown to his son Géza, a boy of ten or eleven.

claims.text: Queen Helena had 68 nobles killed at the assembly of Arad.
claims.note: The number comes from the 14th-century chronicle, written long after. The massacre itself is widely accepted.

claims.text: Béla II drank heavily, and his courtiers took advantage.
claims.note: The chronicle says so; it may be a moralising explanation for a weak reign.

claims.text: The pretender Boris was Coloman's son.
claims.note: Coloman sent his Kievan wife away for adultery before Boris was born. Béla's side called him a bastard, and nobody can settle it.

reigns.hook: Béla the Blind is dead. His son Géza is a child, so his mother Helena and uncle Beloš will run Hungary for him, with Germans to the west and Byzantium to the south.

reigns.tagline: Boy king, crusaders, Saxons and a Byzantine headache
reigns.cameToPower: Succeeded his father as a boy
reigns.previously: Béla the Blind dies, leaving a boy on the throne.
paragraphs: Géza was about ten when his father died, so his mother Helena and her brother Beloš ran things. In 1146, at about 16, he led his army against the Austrians and smashed them on the Fischa river. A year later the Second Crusade tramped through: first King Conrad III of Germany, then Louis VII of France, who got on far better with his hosts.
Géza also invited settlers from the German lands to farm and guard the empty south of Transylvania. They became the Transylvanian Saxons, and their towns and fortified churches still stand.

The big worry was Byzantium. Emperor Manuel I, whose mother was a daughter of Ladislaus I, wanted Hungary under his thumb. Géza's own brothers Ladislaus and Stephen went over to Manuel, and the wars dragged on through the 1150s. Géza died on 31 May 1162, and his teenage son Stephen was crowned.

claims.text: Géza II invited German 'guests' to settle in Transylvania.
claims.note: Andrew II's charter for the Saxons in 1224 looks back to settlers called in by King Géza.

claims.text: The teenage Géza beat the Austrians on the Fischa in 1146.
claims.note: Otto of Freising, brother of the beaten Austrian duke, describes the defeat in his chronicle.

claims.text: Emperor Manuel I was half Hungarian.
claims.note: His mother, Empress Irene, was born Piroska, a daughter of King Ladislaus I.

reigns.hook: Géza II dies young. His son Stephen is barely 15, and Emperor Manuel has two of the boy's uncles ready to take his place.

reigns.tagline: Fifteen, crowned, and chased out by his own uncles
reigns.previously: Géza II dies. Two of his brothers are waiting in Constantinople.
paragraphs: Stephen was fifteen when his father died, and Archbishop Lucas of Esztergom crowned him at once. That should have settled it. But the Byzantine emperor Manuel I was sheltering two of the boy's uncles, Ladislaus and Stephen, and he wanted a friendly king in Hungary. His money and threats did the rest. Within weeks the barons had dropped the teenager. His men were beaten at Kapuvár, and Stephen fled to Austria.

He did not give up. When his uncle Ladislaus died in January 1163, Stephen gathered loyal lords and German troops and beat the other uncle, Stephen IV, at Székesfehérvár on 19 June 1163. Manuel then switched tactics. He took Stephen's younger brother Béla to Constantinople as his heir and claimed Béla's lands in the south along with him.
Fighting over Syrmium and Dalmatia dragged on for years. In 1167 Manuel's army crushed the Hungarians near Zimony, and the south was lost. Stephen died on 4 March 1172, aged about 24, with no son.

claims.text: Stephen III was poisoned.
claims.note: Rumour at the time pointed at people close to Byzantium. Nothing proves it, and a young man could die of many things in 1172.

claims.text: Archbishop Lucas refused to crown his rivals and stood by Stephen.
claims.note: Lucas excommunicated the anti-king Ladislaus II; papal letters and the chronicle show his loyalty.

claims.text: Manuel I made Stephen's brother Béla his own heir.
claims.note: The Byzantine historians Kinnamos and Choniates both record Béla's new name, Alexios, and his engagement to Manuel's daughter.

reigns.hook: Go back to the summer of 1162. The uncle who chased the boy king out is Ladislaus, Manuel's candidate, and he needs a bishop willing to put the crown on his head.

reigns.tagline: Byzantium's man held the crown for six months
reigns.previously: Stephen III is crowned at 15. Byzantium backs his uncles instead.
paragraphs: Ladislaus was a younger son of Béla the Blind. He had quarrelled with his brother Géza II and gone off to Constantinople, where Emperor Manuel I made him welcome. When Géza died, Manuel saw his chance. He first pushed Ladislaus's brother Stephen for the throne, but the Hungarian lords would not have him. Ladislaus, older and less tied to Byzantium, was easier to swallow.

Archbishop Lucas of Esztergom refused to crown him. So the Archbishop of Kalocsa did it instead, in July 1162, and Lucas excommunicated the new king for his trouble. Ladislaus had Lucas locked up. He named his brother Stephen his heir, but he had little time to enjoy the crown. He died on 14 January 1163, after about six months as king.

claims.text: Archbishop Lucas excommunicated Ladislaus II.
claims.note: The chronicle and papal correspondence record it. Pope Alexander III later pressed for Lucas to be freed.

claims.text: Manuel I argued that in Hungary the crown passed to a dead king's brothers.
claims.note: John Kinnamos, Manuel's secretary, records the argument. It suited Byzantium; Hungarian custom had in fact been mixed.

claims.text: The Hungarian lords preferred Ladislaus because his brother Stephen was too close to Manuel.
claims.note: This is how Byzantine writers explain the choice. Hungarian sources say little about the bargaining.

reigns.hook: Ladislaus is dead, and the crown passes to the uncle the Hungarians liked even less: Stephen, married to the emperor's own niece.

reigns.tagline: The emperor's nephew-in-law lasted five months
reigns.previously: Ladislaus II dies after barely six months as king.
paragraphs: Stephen was the youngest son of Béla the Blind. He had plotted against his brother Géza II, fled to Constantinople, and married Maria Komnene, niece of Emperor Manuel I. To Hungarians he was Byzantium's puppet, and he behaved like one. When Ladislaus II died in January 1163, Stephen took the crown, and the barons began slipping away almost at once.

On 19 June 1163 his nephew Stephen III beat him at Székesfehérvár. He was captured, let go, and ran back to Manuel. He tried again with Byzantine help and dug in at Zimony on the Danube. Stephen III besieged the town, and on 11 April 1165 Stephen IV died there, reportedly poisoned by his own men. The town fell soon after.

claims.text: Stephen IV was poisoned by followers bribed by Stephen III.
claims.note: The Byzantine historian Kinnamos says so. He was writing for Manuel's court and had every reason to blame the Hungarian king.

claims.text: Stephen IV was married to Emperor Manuel I's niece Maria Komnene.
claims.note: Byzantine sources record the marriage, which bound him tightly to Manuel's plans for Hungary.

reigns.hook: Both uncles are gone. Stephen III dies seven years later with no son. His brother Béla, raised in Constantinople as the emperor's heir, packs for home.

reigns.tagline: Nearly a Byzantine emperor, then a very rich king
reigns.previously: Stephen III outlasts both uncles, then dies at about 24 with no son.
paragraphs: Béla grew up in Constantinople as a hostage who became a favourite. Emperor Manuel I renamed him Alexios, engaged him to his daughter Maria and treated him as his heir. Then Manuel had a son, and the plan was dropped. When Stephen III died, Manuel sent Béla home with his blessing.

The Archbishop of Esztergom refused to crown a man he saw as a Greek puppet, so the Archbishop of Kalocsa did it instead, in January 1173. Béla turned out to be a strong king. He took back Dalmatia after Manuel died, had business at court written down, and in 1186 married Margaret, sister of King Philip II of France. A list of his income makes him look as rich as any king in the West.
He died on 23 April 1196. In 1848 workmen at Székesfehérvár found his tomb untouched, his skeleton still wearing its crown.

claims.text: Béla III's yearly income matched the kings of France and England.
claims.note: A Latin list of his revenues, kept in Paris, gives huge figures. Historians doubt what it counted, and some think it was inflated to impress.

claims.text: Béla was set to inherit the Byzantine Empire.
claims.note: Byzantine historians John Kinnamos and Niketas Choniates record his title and betrothal, ended when Manuel's son was born in 1169.

claims.text: His tomb was found intact at Székesfehérvár in 1848.
claims.note: The remains were reburied in Matthias Church, Budapest, in 1898.

reigns.hook: Béla leaves two sons. The elder, Emeric, gets the crown. The younger, Andrew, gets money for a crusade, and he has no intention of spending it on one.

reigns.tagline: He walked unarmed into his rebel brother's camp
reigns.previously: Béla III dies rich, with two sons who can't stand each other.
paragraphs: Emeric had been crowned while his father was still alive, so the throne was his. His younger brother Andrew got money to go on crusade and spent it on an army instead. In 1197 Andrew beat Emeric and forced him to hand over Croatia and Dalmatia. Emeric hit back and routed Andrew at Rád in 1199, but the feud kept flaring up, with the Pope trying to make peace between them.

In 1202 the knights of the Fourth Crusade, deep in debt to Venice, captured Zara on Emeric's own Adriatic coast. In 1203 the brothers' armies faced each other near Varasd. Emeric took off his weapons, walked into Andrew's camp alone and led him away a prisoner, or so the story goes.
Then Emeric fell ill. He had his small son crowned as Ladislaus III on 26 August 1204, made peace with Andrew and named him the boy's guardian. He died on 30 November 1204.

claims.text: Emeric walked unarmed into Andrew's camp and arrested him.
claims.note: Thomas of Split tells it in the 13th century. It is a good story with no other witness.

claims.text: Crusaders captured Zara, a Christian city under Hungarian rule, in 1202.
claims.note: Villehardouin, who was there, describes it. Pope Innocent III excommunicated the crusaders for it.

claims.text: Andrew paid for his rebellion with the money his father left him for a crusade.
claims.note: Béla III's bequest is well recorded, and Andrew never went east until 1217.

reigns.hook: Emeric is dead. On the throne sits a crowned little boy. His guardian is the uncle who spent seven years trying to take the crown, and the queen does not trust him at all.

reigns.tagline: A little king smuggled abroad with the Holy Crown
reigns.previously: Emeric dies, leaving a crowned little boy and a hungry brother.
paragraphs: Ladislaus was about four when his father died. He had already been crowned, so on paper he was king. In practice his uncle Andrew, his guardian, ran the kingdom and helped himself to the money Emeric had set aside for the boy. His mother, Constance of Aragon, decided they were not safe.

She slipped out of Hungary with her son and the Holy Crown and took refuge with Duke Leopold VI of Austria. Andrew was furious and talked of war. It never came to that. On 7 May 1205 the little king died in Vienna. Leopold sent the crown back to Hungary, and Constance went home to Aragon. A few years later she married the young Frederick II and ended up Holy Roman Empress.

claims.text: Queen Constance fled to Austria with her son and the Holy Crown.
claims.note: Hungarian and Austrian sources agree. The crown was handed back after the boy's death.

claims.text: Andrew seized money Emeric had left for his son.
claims.note: The charge is repeated in later accounts. How much was taken, and whether Andrew saw it as theft, is unclear.

claims.text: Constance of Aragon later married Emperor Frederick II.
claims.note: They married in 1209; she was crowned empress in Rome in 1220.

reigns.hook: The boy king is dead in Vienna and the Holy Crown is on its way back. Andrew, after nine years of trying, finally gets it. He has a lot of friends to reward.

reigns.tagline: The big spender who signed Hungary's Magna Carta
reigns.cameToPower: His nephew the boy king died
reigns.previously: Little Ladislaus III dies in Austria. His uncle Andrew is waiting.
paragraphs: Andrew gave away royal land like there was no tomorrow, calling his gifts a new policy. His German queen Gertrude of Merania pushed her relatives into top jobs. In 1213, while Andrew was away at war, a group of nobles murdered her. That killing became the play and opera Bánk bán, a national classic.

In 1217 he led a crusade to the Holy Land, stayed a few months, and came home with relics and debts. In 1222 the angry lesser nobles forced the Golden Bull on him, Hungary's Magna Carta. It protected their rights and even let them resist a king who broke it.

He called in the Teutonic Knights to guard Transylvania, then threw them out in 1225 when they tried to answer only to the Pope. His daughter Elizabeth became one of the most popular saints in Europe. He died on 21 September 1235.

claims.text: The archbishop sent a letter that could read 'kill the queen' or 'don't kill the queen'.
claims.note: A Latin sentence with no commas, said to be from Archbishop John. It turns up in later chroniclers; no original survives.

claims.text: The nobleman Bánk led the plot to kill Gertrude.
claims.note: Sources disagree on who did it; Bánk's starring role was fixed by later writers and Katona's play.

claims.text: The Golden Bull gave nobles the right to resist the king.
claims.note: Its closing clause says so. The right was dropped only in 1687.

reigns.hook: Andrew is dead. His son Béla can't wait to take back everything his father gave away. Far to the east, a Mongol army is on the move.

reigns.tagline: The Mongols wrecked his country, so he built it again
reigns.reignEnded: Died after war with his son
reigns.previously: Andrew II dies, having given away half the royal lands.
paragraphs: Béla was out to restore royal power, and the nobles hated him for it. Then he took in tens of thousands of Cumans fleeing the Mongols, nomads who trampled crops and quarrelled with everyone. When the Mongols came in 1241, a mob in Pest murdered the Cuman khan Köten, and his people rode off, burning as they went.

On 11 April 1241 the Mongols destroyed Béla's army at Muhi on the Sajó river. Béla fled all the way to the Adriatic and hid near Trogir and on an island off the coast, while the Mongols burned the country. In 1242 they suddenly turned back east. The Great Khan Ögedei had died.

Béla rebuilt with stone castles, new towns and settlers, earning the name second founder of the state. He gave his daughter Margaret to a convent, as he had vowed. His last years were spent at war with his own son Stephen. He died on 3 May 1270.

claims.text: The Mongols left Hungary because Ögedei had died.
claims.note: That's the classic explanation. Some historians point to losses, bad pasture or a flooded, starving land instead.

claims.text: Béla vowed his unborn daughter Margaret to God if Hungary was saved.
claims.note: Her early Lives say so. She lived on the Danube island now called Margaret Island, and was made a saint in 1943.

claims.text: Up to half of Hungary's people died in the Mongol invasion.
claims.note: Master Roger's eyewitness account is grim; modern guesses range from about 15 to 50 per cent.

reigns.hook: Béla is dead, and his son Stephen V finally has the throne he fought for. He will hold it for barely two years. The last Árpáds are running out of time.

reigns.previously: Béla IV dies, worn out by wars with the Mongols and his own son.
paragraphs: Stephen was crowned junior king as a small child and never liked waiting. In 1253 he married Elizabeth, daughter of a Cuman chieftain, which tied the royal family to the nomads his father had let in. In the 1260s he and Béla IV fought an open civil war. In March 1265 Stephen beat his father's army at Isaszeg, and Hungary stayed split between the two of them until the old king died.

When Stephen finally took over, his sister Anna fled to Prague with much of the royal treasure. Her son-in-law, King Ottokar II of Bohemia, went to war, and a peace was signed at Pressburg in 1271. In 1272 a rebel baron, Joachim Gutkeled, kidnapped Stephen's ten-year-old son Ladislaus. Stephen fell ill while trying to get him back and died on Csepel Island on 6 August 1272.

claims.text: Stephen beat his own father's army at Isaszeg in 1265.
claims.note: Royal charters praise the barons who fought for Stephen there. The war between father and son is well documented.

claims.text: Stephen's sister Anna carried off the royal treasure to Bohemia.
claims.note: Hungarian sources complain of it, and the treasure was still a sore point in the peace talks with Ottokar.

claims.text: His daughter Mary married into the royal family of Naples.
claims.note: She married the future Charles II of Naples. Her grandson Charles Robert would claim Hungary through her.

reigns.hook: Stephen is dead, and his son Ladislaus is ten years old and in the hands of the man who kidnapped him. The barons now own the king.

reigns.tagline: The king who lived like a Cuman and died like one
reigns.previously: Stephen V dies while his little son is held by a rebel baron.
paragraphs: Ladislaus became king at ten, and the great families fought over him like a prize. As he grew up he chose his own side: his mother's people, the Cumans. On 26 August 1278 his horsemen helped Rudolf of Habsburg beat King Ottokar of Bohemia on the Marchfeld, a battle that set the Habsburgs up in Austria for six centuries.

Then came the papal legate, Philip of Fermo, who in 1279 demanded the Cumans settle down, leave their tents and become proper Christians. Ladislaus agreed, then wriggled out, and was excommunicated. He crushed a Cuman revolt at Lake Hód in 1282 and faced a second Mongol invasion in 1285.
He dressed like a Cuman, kept Cuman companions and shut his queen in a convent. On 10 July 1290 Cuman killers murdered him in his tent at Kőrösszeg. He was 27 and had no children.

claims.text: Ladislaus lived openly with Cuman mistresses and turned his back on his queen.
claims.note: Church writers and a furious Pope said so. They wanted him gone, but his queen's confinement is on record.

claims.text: His horsemen helped Rudolf of Habsburg win the Marchfeld in 1278.
claims.note: Austrian and Hungarian sources agree that the Hungarian and Cuman cavalry mattered.

claims.text: Simon of Kéza wrote his history of the Hungarians for Ladislaus.
claims.note: Simon, a court cleric, dedicated the Gesta Hungarorum to him in the 1280s.

reigns.hook: Ladislaus dies childless. The best claim now belongs to a man raised in Venice, a grandson of Andrew II whose own uncles called his father a bastard.

reigns.tagline: Raised in Venice, he was the last of Árpád's line
reigns.previously: Cumans murder Ladislaus IV in his tent. He leaves no children.
paragraphs: Andrew's father, Stephen the Posthumous, was born after Andrew II died, and his half-brothers swore he was no son of the king. Stephen settled in Venice and married into the Morosini family, so Andrew grew up a Venetian. When Ladislaus IV was murdered, the Archbishop of Esztergom backed him, and he was crowned at Székesfehérvár on 23 July 1290.

Rivals lined up at once. Rudolf of Habsburg claimed Hungary for his son Albert, and Andrew marched on Vienna in 1291 to settle that. Queen Mary of Naples, Stephen V's daughter, claimed it for her own son. Meanwhile the great lords carved out provinces of their own. Andrew died in Buda on 14 January 1301, aged about 35. He left a daughter, Elizabeth, and no son.

claims.text: Andrew III was poisoned.
claims.note: Rumours went round at once. There is no proof, and he may simply have fallen ill.

claims.text: Andrew's father was not really Andrew II's son.
claims.note: Béla IV and his brother called Stephen the Posthumous illegitimate, but they had every reason to. Most historians accept him as Andrew II's son.

claims.text: Andrew marched to Vienna in 1291 and forced peace on Albert of Austria.
claims.note: The Peace of Hainburg in August 1291 ended the war on terms good for Hungary.

reigns.hook: The Árpád male line is gone after four hundred years. A twelve-year-old prince from Naples is already in the country, and the Pope is on his side.

reigns.title: Charles Robert, Pretender
reigns.tagline: Crowned with the wrong crown in the wrong town
reigns.previously: Andrew III dies. The Árpád male line is gone.
paragraphs: Charles Robert was the grandson of Queen Mary of Naples, Stephen V's daughter. In August 1300, aged about twelve, he landed at Split with the backing of the Croatian lord Paul Šubić. When Andrew III died a few months later, Charles hurried to Esztergom, where the archbishop-elect, Gregory Bicskei, crowned him before mid-May 1301.

It did not count for much. The Holy Crown was not used, and Székesfehérvár was not the place. Most barons wanted someone else and chose the son of the King of Bohemia. Charles fell back to the south. The Pope backed him all the way, and in 1303 Boniface VIII ruled in his favour. On 10 October 1307 an assembly on the field of Rákos accepted him. On 27 November 1308 the barons elected him at Pest.

claims.text: Charles's first coronation in 1301 used a makeshift crown.
claims.note: The Holy Crown was out of reach. Hungarians held that only the Holy Crown, at Székesfehérvár, made a lawful king.

claims.text: Pope Boniface VIII ruled in 1303 that Charles was the rightful king.
claims.note: The papal bull survives. It did little to change minds in Hungary at first.

reigns.hook: Most of the barons look the other way: to Prague, where the King of Bohemia has an eleven-year-old son engaged to Andrew III's daughter.

reigns.previously: A boy from Naples has the Pope. Most barons want someone else.
paragraphs: Wenceslaus was the son of King Wenceslaus II of Bohemia, and he was engaged to Andrew III's daughter Elizabeth. The barons who did not want an Angevin offered him the throne. On 27 August 1301 he was crowned at Székesfehérvár with the Holy Crown. He took a Hungarian royal name and was crowned as Ladislaus.

He was eleven, and the real players were his father's advisers and the great lords. Charles Robert's camp grew stronger. In 1304 Wenceslaus II marched in with an army and took his son home to Bohemia, bringing the Holy Crown with them. When the boy became King of Bohemia in 1305, he gave up Hungary. On 9 October 1305 he passed his claim, and the crown, to Otto of Bavaria. The next August he was murdered in Olomouc.

claims.text: Wenceslaus was crowned King of Hungary under the name Ladislaus.
claims.note: The Illuminated Chronicle and charters of his reign use the name.

claims.text: His father carried off the Holy Crown to Prague in 1304.
claims.note: Hungarian and Czech chronicles agree, and it went on to Otto from there.

claims.text: Wenceslaus was killed in Olomouc on the orders of an enemy.
claims.note: Nobody was ever convicted. Suspects ranged from Polish rivals to the Habsburgs, and none is proven.

reigns.hook: The claim now belongs to a Bavarian duke who is Béla IV's grandson. All Otto has to do is get himself and the Holy Crown into Hungary in one piece.

reigns.tagline: He lost the Holy Crown on the road, then lost it for good
reigns.previously: Wenceslaus goes home to Bohemia and hands his claim to Otto.
paragraphs: Otto III, Duke of Lower Bavaria, had a Hungarian mother, a daughter of Béla IV. The Habsburgs were watching the roads, so he slipped into Hungary in disguise with the Holy Crown. The chronicle says it was hidden in a flask, fell off on the way and was found again by luck. On 6 December 1305 two bishops crowned him at Székesfehérvár.

He had the crown but little else. The burghers of Buda liked him, the great lords mostly did not. In 1307 he rode to Transylvania to win over its strongman, the voivode Ladislaus Kán, by marrying his daughter. Kán locked him up instead and kept the Holy Crown. Kán let him go some months later, and he went home to Bavaria, where he called himself King of Hungary until he died in 1312.

claims.text: Otto lost the Holy Crown on the road while carrying it in a flask.
claims.note: The Illuminated Chronicle tells it, with a picture. It may be a garbled version of a real mishap.

claims.text: Otto crossed into Hungary disguised as a merchant.
claims.note: Told in the chronicles to explain how he got past Habsburg guards. The detail cannot be checked.

claims.text: Ladislaus Kán held the Holy Crown until 1310.
claims.note: Charles Robert had to use a stand-in crown in 1309; the papal legate's records cover the deal to get it back.

reigns.hook: Otto slinks home to Bavaria with no crown. Hungary's barons, prodded by a papal legate, are finally ready to give Charles Robert the throne.

reigns.tagline: Crowned three times, and the gold kept coming
reigns.previously: Otto loses the Holy Crown to a Transylvanian lord and slinks home.
paragraphs: Charles Robert of Anjou was crowned three times: in 1301, in 1309 with a stand-in, and finally with the Holy Crown on 27 August 1310, once Kán handed it over. Then he set about breaking the little kings. He beat the Aba family at Rozgonyi in 1312 and picked off the rest one by one. Matthew Csák held out until his death in 1321.

Hungary's gold mines at Kremnica were among the richest in Europe, and Charles cashed in. From 1325 he minted gold florins of steady value. On 17 April 1330, at dinner at Visegrád, the nobleman Felician Záh drew a sword on the royal family and cut off four fingers of Queen Elizabeth's hand. Felician was killed on the spot, and his whole family was punished with him.
That autumn Charles invaded Wallachia and was ambushed in a mountain pass at Posada; he barely escaped. In 1335 he hosted the kings of Bohemia and Poland at Visegrád. He died there on 16 July 1342.

claims.text: Felician Záh attacked because the queen's brother Casimir had seduced his daughter.
claims.note: The explanation turns up only in later Polish and Italian writers; Hungarian sources of the time give no motive.

claims.text: Záh's whole family was punished for the attack.
claims.note: The court ruled that his kin to the third degree be wiped out; his daughter was mutilated and others executed.

claims.text: At Posada a loyal knight swapped armour with Charles and died in his place.
claims.note: The Illuminated Chronicle tells it and paints the battle; there is no other witness.

reigns.hook: Charles leaves his son Louis a full treasury and a peaceful kingdom. In Naples, Louis's little brother Andrew is married to the heiress Joanna. Some there want him gone.

reigns.tagline: The avenging king who ruled from the Baltic to the Adriatic
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Eldest surviving son of Charles I
reigns.previously: Charles Robert dies at Visegrád, leaving a rich, tamed kingdom.
paragraphs: Louis was sixteen and inherited a full treasury. Then family business took over. His younger brother Andrew had been married off to Queen Joanna of Naples. In 1345 Andrew was dragged from his bed at Aversa and strangled with a cord. Louis blamed Joanna's court and marched on Naples twice, in 1347 and 1350. He took the city, executed a cousin he suspected, and was driven home as much by the Black Death as by anyone's army.

Closer to home he did better. Wars with Venice ended in 1358 with all of Dalmatia handed to Hungary. In 1370 his uncle Casimir the Great died and Louis became King of Poland too. On paper his realm ran from the Baltic to the Adriatic. He founded a university at Pécs and fixed noble land law for centuries.

His great gap was a son. Louis had three daughters, and one died young. So he spent his last years bargaining to get Mary accepted in Hungary and Poland. He died at Nagyszombat in 1382, and the two crowns split at once.

claims.text: Queen Joanna had a hand in her husband Andrew's murder.
claims.note: Louis was sure of it. A papal inquiry cleared her, and historians still argue over who gave the order.

claims.text: Louis suffered from leprosy in his last years.
claims.note: Later writers say he had a disfiguring skin disease. The contemporary evidence is thin and the diagnosis is a guess.

claims.text: The 1351 law tied noble land to the family forever.
claims.note: The law on 'aviticitas' meant estates could not be sold outside the kin. It lasted until 1848.

reigns.hook: Louis is gone and Hungary has never had a queen in her own right. So the nobles find a workaround: they crown eleven-year-old Mary as their King.

reigns.tagline: The girl crowned King, then dethroned, then caged
reigns.previously: Louis the Great dies without a son. His daughters inherit his crowns.
paragraphs: Mary was eleven when she was crowned at Székesfehérvár, and she was crowned King, since the law had no slot for a ruling queen. The real power was her mother, Elizabeth of Bosnia, and the palatine Nicholas Garai. Mary had been promised to Sigismund of Luxembourg. Her mother kept stalling the wedding, and the nobles who wanted a grown man on the throne started looking south. Sigismund forced the marriage in October 1385, too late.

In late 1385 Charles of Durazzo, King of Naples, sailed in. Mary had to step aside, and he was crowned on 31 December. Five weeks later he was cut down in the queens' own rooms. Mary was back, but not for long. In July 1386 rebels ambushed the queens at Gorjani in Slavonia, killed Garai and dragged them to the castle of Novigrad. There, in January 1387, Elizabeth was strangled.

The barons crowned Sigismund on 31 March 1387, and Venetian ships freed Mary that June. She reigned beside him, more name than power, until she fell from her horse while pregnant and died on 17 May 1395.

claims.text: Mary was crowned King of Hungary, not queen.
claims.note: Charters call her 'rex'. Hungarian law only knew a king, so the title was the price of having her.

claims.text: Elizabeth was strangled in front of her daughter.
claims.note: The murder in Novigrad is certain. The detail that Mary watched comes from later accounts and can't be checked.

claims.text: Mary's death was a riding accident.
claims.note: Chronicles agree she fell from her horse while heavily pregnant and died soon after, along with the baby.

reigns.hook: Rewind to the winter of 1385. A short, smiling cousin from Naples has just landed, and Hungary's barons are ready to make him king over Mary's head.

reigns.tagline: Thirty-nine days a king, then a sword to the head
reigns.reignEnded: Struck down in the queens' rooms
reigns.previously: Mary is queen in name. Her mother rules, and the barons are restless.
paragraphs: Charles of Durazzo was already King Charles III of Naples. He had grown up at Louis the Great's court and had taken Naples by force in 1381, where Queen Joanna died in his prison. Hungarians called him Charles the Small because he was short. A party of southern nobles wanted a man in charge, and in 1385 he answered their call.

He reached Buda, Mary gave way, and he was crowned at Székesfehérvár on 31 December 1385. The queens had to stand by and watch. On 7 February 1386 they invited him to their rooms. While he read a letter, the cupbearer Blaise Forgách drew a sword and struck him in the head. Charles was carried off to Visegrád as a prisoner and died of his wounds on 24 February.

claims.text: The queens set the trap themselves.
claims.note: Charles was attacked in Elizabeth's rooms with Garai's men ready. Most historians think she planned it, but no order survives.

claims.text: Charles was strangled or poisoned in prison to finish the job.
claims.note: Some writers say so. Others say the wound simply killed him. Either way he never left Visegrád.

claims.text: Queen Joanna of Naples was killed on Charles's orders.
claims.note: She died in his custody in 1382, probably smothered or strangled. The order is assumed, not proved.

reigns.hook: Charles is dead, but his friends want revenge. The queens are about to be ambushed on the road, and Mary's husband Sigismund is the only man who can rescue the crown.

reigns.tagline: Fifty years, five crowns and one Order of the Dragon
reigns.cameToPower: Crowned by a league of barons
reigns.previously: Charles the Small is dead. Rebels are about to seize the queens.
paragraphs: Sigismund was nineteen, foreign and broke when the barons crowned him. He paid them in royal castles and spent years learning who really ran Hungary. In 1396 he led a huge crusade against the Ottomans and watched it fall apart at Nicopolis. He escaped down the Danube by boat. In 1401 his own barons locked him up for months. He came out, made deals and built a loyal circle.

In 1408 he and Queen Barbara founded the Order of the Dragon, a club for his closest allies. One member was a Wallachian prince who became Vlad Dracul, father of Dracula. Then Sigismund went big. He became King of the Romans, ran the Council of Constance that ended the papal schism, and let Jan Hus burn there in 1415. He became King of Bohemia, and in 1433 emperor.

Meanwhile the Ottoman border crept north, Dalmatia was sold to Venice by a rival, and Hussite raiders hit Upper Hungary. Sigismund had no son. His daughter Elizabeth was married to Albert of Austria, and that is where the crown went.

claims.text: Vlad Dracul took his name from Sigismund's Order of the Dragon.
claims.note: Vlad II was admitted in 1431. 'Dracul' means dragon, and his son Vlad the Impaler signed as 'Dracula', son of the Dragon.

claims.text: Sigismund told a priest who corrected his Latin: 'I am King of the Romans, and above grammar.'
claims.note: A famous anecdote set at Constance and retold for centuries. There's no reliable record that he said it.

claims.text: He broke his promise of safe passage to Jan Hus.
claims.note: Hus came to Constance with Sigismund's safe-conduct and was burnt on 6 July 1415. Sigismund argued that heretics had no protection.

reigns.hook: Sigismund dies at Znojmo. Hungary takes his son-in-law Albert, a Habsburg, but makes him promise to live among them and fight the Turks.

reigns.tagline: The first Habsburg king, gone in under two years
reigns.cameToPower: Elected, crowned on New Year's Day
reigns.previously: Sigismund dies at Znojmo, leaving one daughter and no son.
paragraphs: Albert was already Duke of Austria. He had married Sigismund's daughter Elizabeth, and the Hungarian lords elected him in December 1437. He was crowned on 1 January 1438, the first Habsburg on the Hungarian throne. Within months he was also King of Bohemia and, as Albert II, King of the Romans. The Hungarians made him swear to put their country first and not to hand offices to Germans.

In 1439 the Ottomans took Smederevo, the Serbian fortress on the Danube. Albert gathered an army at Titel, but it melted away while dysentery spread through the camp. He caught it, turned for Vienna, and died at Neszmély on 27 October 1439, aged 42. His wife was pregnant. If the baby was a boy, he would be king.

claims.text: Albert brought on his fatal illness by gorging on melons.
claims.note: Told by chroniclers to explain a sudden death. Dysentery was already ravaging his camp, which explains it fine.

claims.text: He was the first Habsburg King of Hungary.
claims.note: The Habsburgs would hold the crown again from 1526 to 1918.

reigns.tagline: The boy king who charged the sultan and vanished
reigns.previously: Albert dies of dysentery. His widow is due any day.
paragraphs: Władysław III of Poland was fifteen when Hungary's nobles invited him in 1440. They wanted a king who could fight. Queen Elizabeth had other ideas and had the Holy Crown stolen for her baby son. So Vladislaus was crowned in July with a crown taken off St Stephen's reliquary. Civil war followed until Elizabeth died in 1442.

His best weapon was John Hunyadi. In 1443 they went deep into the Balkans on the 'long campaign' and won fight after fight. In 1444 a ten-year peace with Sultan Murad II was agreed at Szeged. Weeks later the papal legate told the king that oaths to infidels did not bind, and the crusade marched again.
On 10 November 1444, at Varna on the Black Sea, the young king charged Murad's janissaries with his guard. He was cut down. His head was put on a lance, and his body was never found. He was twenty.

claims.text: Vladislaus survived Varna and lived out his life in Portugal.
claims.note: A knight called Henrique Alemão on Madeira was later said to be him. There is no real evidence, but the story never quite died.

claims.text: He broke a sworn peace to start the Varna campaign.
claims.note: Cardinal Cesarini released him from the oath. Historians still argue whether the peace had ever been properly sworn.

claims.text: He was crowned with a crown taken from St Stephen's reliquary.
claims.note: With the Holy Crown gone, his supporters borrowed the crown from the saint's head reliquary in Székesfehérvár.

reigns.hook: A baby king in Austria, and two years of chaos. The nobles turn to the war hero who survived Varna. John Hunyadi, son of a Wallachian knight, is about to rule Hungary.

reigns.title: John Hunyadi
reigns.tagline: The White Knight who kept the Turks out of Hungary
reigns.previously: Vladislaus I falls at Varna. His body is never found.
paragraphs: John Hunyadi's father was a minor Wallachian knight given the castle of Hunyad by Sigismund. John rose by fighting. By the 1440s he was the richest landowner in Hungary and its best general. The Turks called him Yanko. Europe called him the White Knight. In June 1446 the diet made him governor for the absent child king, Ladislaus V.

He wasn't always lucky. At Kosovo in 1448 he lost a three-day battle, and on the way home he was held prisoner by the Serbian despot. When Ladislaus came home in 1453 Hunyadi gave up the governorship, keeping his castles and his army.

In July 1456 Mehmed II, fresh from taking Constantinople, besieged Belgrade. Hunyadi broke through on the Danube, crusaders poured out, and the sultan retreated wounded. Three weeks later, on 11 August, Hunyadi died of plague in the camp.

claims.text: Hunyadi was secretly King Sigismund's son.
claims.note: A story spread in the 15th century, perhaps to explain his rise. No evidence backs it.

claims.text: Europe's noon bells celebrate the victory at Belgrade.
claims.note: Pope Callixtus III ordered the bells before the battle to call for prayer. When the victory came, people read them as a victory peal.

claims.text: Hunyadi died of plague just after Belgrade.
claims.note: Plague broke out in the crusader camp. He died at Zimony on 11 August 1456.

reigns.hook: Hunyadi is dead, but the boy king he served is a stranger. Rewind to 1440: Ladislaus V was a baby smuggled out with the Holy Crown.

reigns.tagline: Crowned at twelve weeks with a stolen crown
reigns.previously: Hunyadi saves Belgrade, then dies of plague in the camp.
paragraphs: Ladislaus was born on 22 February 1440, four months after his father died. The day before, his mother's lady-in-waiting, Helene Kottanner, had crept into Visegrád castle, filed through the locks and smuggled the Holy Crown out in a cushion. On 15 May the baby was crowned with it. Kottanner later wrote down the whole adventure.

But the nobles had chosen Vladislaus of Poland, and after Varna Hunyadi ruled. Ladislaus grew up in Austria in the hands of Emperor Frederick III, who also kept the crown. Only in 1452 did rebels force the emperor to let him go.

Back in Hungary Ladislaus fell in with Hunyadi's enemies. In 1456 his kinsman and chief adviser Ulrich of Cilli was killed by Hunyadi's elder son Ladislaus at Belgrade. The king had the young man beheaded in Buda in March 1457 and took his brother Matthias prisoner. Months later, aged 17, the king suddenly died in Prague.

claims.text: Helene Kottanner stole the Holy Crown from Visegrád for the baby king.
claims.note: Her own memoir describes the night raid in detail. It's one of the earliest memoirs by a woman in German.

claims.text: The executioner needed several blows to behead Ladislaus Hunyadi.
claims.note: Chroniclers say the first strokes failed. A later story that a man who survived three blows was owed a pardon is legend.

claims.text: Ladislaus V was poisoned.
claims.note: Rumours blamed George of Poděbrady. A 1985 study of his bones pointed to leukaemia instead.

reigns.hook: The king is dead in Prague, and his prisoner Matthias Hunyadi is fourteen and stuck there. Back in Pest, a crowd on the frozen Danube is about to shout his name.

reigns.tagline: The raven king with a black army and a dream library
reigns.cameToPower: Elected in Pest while a prisoner
reigns.previously: Ladislaus V dies in Prague at 17, with no heir.
paragraphs: Matthias was fourteen and a hostage in Prague when the nobles elected him on 24 January 1458, helped along by his uncle's army. George of Poděbrady let him go in return for marrying his daughter. Emperor Frederick III still held the Holy Crown, so Matthias bought it back for 80,000 gold florins and was finally crowned in 1464.

He taxed hard and spent it on a standing army of mercenaries, the Black Army. With it he fought Bohemia and the emperor. He kept Vlad the Impaler as his prisoner for years. In 1485 he took Vienna and moved in.

His court in Buda went Italian after he married Beatrice of Naples in 1476. His library, the Corvina, was one of the finest in Europe. He died in Vienna in 1490. His only son, John Corvinus, was illegitimate, and the nobles had other plans.

claims.text: Matthias was proclaimed king by crowds on the frozen Danube.
claims.note: The scene on the ice is a beloved tradition. The election itself happened in Pest, and sources differ on the details.

claims.text: He wandered his kingdom in disguise to see how ordinary people were treated.
claims.note: Folk tales of 'Matthias the Just' grew after his death. The saying 'Dead is King Matthias, gone is justice' came from the same nostalgia.

claims.text: Around 200 Corvina volumes survive, scattered across Europe.
claims.note: The library was looted after 1526. Surviving books sit in Budapest, Vienna, Wolfenbüttel and elsewhere.

reigns.hook: Matthias is dead and his son is passed over. The nobles want a king who says yes to everything, and they know just the man in Prague.

reigns.tagline: King 'Fine', who said yes while the kingdom wore thin
reigns.previously: Matthias dies in Vienna, and his illegitimate son is passed over.
paragraphs: Vladislaus Jagiellon was already King of Bohemia and the son of Ladislaus V's sister. The magnates liked him because he looked easy to manage. They were right. Courtiers joked that he answered every request with the Czech word 'dobře', fine, and he became King Dobře. Matthias's taxes were cut, and the unpaid Black Army fell apart.

In 1514 the archbishop Tamás Bakócz called a crusade against the Turks. Peasants came by the thousand under a soldier named György Dózsa and turned on their lords. John Zápolya crushed them at Temesvár. Dózsa was set on a red-hot iron throne and crowned with a red-hot crown.

That same year István Werbőczy wrote down the noble law, the Tripartitum, which tied peasants to the land for good. In 1515 a double marriage pact with the Habsburgs was sealed in Vienna. Vladislaus died in 1516.

claims.text: Vladislaus answered every request with 'dobře', fine.
claims.note: The nickname was real and widely used. Whether he truly said nothing else is a joke at his expense.

claims.text: Dózsa was executed on a heated iron throne.
claims.note: Contemporary accounts describe it. The story that his followers were forced to eat his flesh is harder to check.

claims.text: The Tripartitum became Hungary's law book for 300 years.
claims.note: It was never formally enacted, but after it was printed in 1517 courts used it until the 19th century.

reigns.hook: The new king is nine and the treasury is empty. In Istanbul, a young sultan named Suleiman will soon be looking north.

reigns.tagline: The boy king who drowned with medieval Hungary
reigns.previously: Vladislaus II dies in Buda, leaving a weak crown to a child.
paragraphs: Louis was born too early in 1506, and his mother died soon after. He was crowned before he was two and was king at nine. The barons fought over his treasury while there was barely any money left. As agreed in 1515, he married Mary of Habsburg, the sister of the future Emperor Charles V.

Suleiman the Magnificent took Belgrade, the key fortress on the Danube, in 1521. Help from the West never came in time. In August 1526 Suleiman marched north with a huge army. Louis met him on the plain at Mohács with about 25,000 men. Zápolya's Transylvanian troops had not arrived.

On 29 August the Hungarian army was destroyed in around two hours. Seven bishops and most of the barons died. Louis fled, and his horse fell crossing the swollen Csele stream. He drowned in his armour, aged twenty, with no children.

claims.text: The premature baby was kept warm inside the carcasses of freshly slaughtered animals.
claims.note: A story told by later writers. Nobody at the time records it.

claims.text: Louis drowned in the Csele stream while fleeing.
claims.note: The chancellor István Brodarics, who fought at Mohács, reports it, and the body was later found in the stream.

claims.text: Louis was murdered by his own nobles, not drowned.
claims.note: A later rumour blamed Zápolya's men. Brodarics's account and the recovered body don't support it.

reigns.hook: No king, no army, and two claimants. John Zápolya, the richest man in Hungary, whose army never reached Mohács, is already heading for the crown.

reigns.tagline: The last native king, saved and sold out by the sultan
reigns.reignEnded: Died two weeks after his son's birth
reigns.previously: Mohács: the army is wiped out and young Louis II drowns as he flees.
paragraphs: John Zápolya was the richest lord in Hungary and voivode of Transylvania. In August 1526 he was marching to join the king, but his army never reached Mohács. After the disaster, the nobles who wanted no more foreign kings rallied to him. On 11 November 1526 he was crowned at Székesfehérvár with the Holy Crown. Within weeks a rival diet at Pozsony chose Ferdinand of Habsburg instead.

Ferdinand's troops drove John out of Buda in 1527, and after another defeat he fled to Poland. With no friends left in Christendom, he turned to the sultan. In 1529 he met Suleiman on the old battlefield of Mohács, and the Turks put him back in Buda on their way to besiege Vienna. Vienna held. For the next decade two crowned kings fought over the wreckage while Ottoman raiders roamed at will.

In 1538 the rivals made a secret deal at Nagyvárad: John would stay king for life, then Ferdinand would get everything. Then John, in his fifties, married Isabella, daughter of the King of Poland. In July 1540 she gave him a son, John Sigismund. Two weeks later John was dead, and his followers hailed the baby as king. The secret deal was dead too.

claims.text: Zápolya held his army back from Mohács on purpose, hoping the king would fall.
claims.note: His enemies said so after the battle. His troops were still days away, and many historians blame confused orders and the royal army's haste to fight.

claims.text: Zápolya kissed Suleiman's hand when they met at Mohács in 1529.
claims.note: Ottoman accounts make a show of his submission; Hungarian writers played it down. How humbling the meeting really was depends on whose chronicle you read.

claims.text: The Treaty of Nagyvárad promised Ferdinand the whole kingdom after John's death.
claims.note: The treaty text survives. It was kept secret, and John's party ignored it once his son was born.

reigns.hook: Suleiman comes to protect the baby king. In 1541 he takes Buda for himself, and Ferdinand is left with a strip of a broken kingdom.

reigns.tagline: The Habsburg who won a third of a kingdom
reigns.cameToPower: Elected by a rival diet, crowned 1527
reigns.previously: John Zápolya dies, and his followers hail his baby son as king.
paragraphs: Ferdinand's claim came through his wife Anne, Louis II's sister, and old treaties between the Jagiellons and the Habsburgs. A diet at Pozsony elected him in December 1526, and on 3 November 1527 he was crowned at Székesfehérvár, almost a year after John. Hungary now had two crowned kings and a civil war that would last until John died.

In 1541 Ferdinand tried to grab Buda. Suleiman marched in to protect the baby John Sigismund, and on 29 August his men walked into the city and kept it. The kingdom broke in three: Royal Hungary, a Habsburg strip in the north and west; Ottoman Hungary in the middle; and Transylvania, a principality under Queen Isabella and her son that paid tribute to the sultan.

The border war never stopped. In 1552 the small garrison of Eger, led by István Dobó, held off a vast Ottoman army for over five weeks. With Székesfehérvár in Turkish hands from 1543, Pozsony (today's Bratislava) became the capital and later the coronation city. In 1558 Ferdinand followed his brother Charles V as Holy Roman Emperor.

claims.text: The women of Eger poured boiling pitch and hot soup on the Turks scaling the walls.
claims.note: The poet Sebestyén Tinódi, writing in 1553, praises women fighting on the walls. The vivid details were made famous by Géza Gárdonyi's 1899 novel, Eclipse of the Crescent Moon.

claims.text: The Turks took Buda by a trick, strolling in as sightseers while the baby king was in the sultan's camp.
claims.note: Hungarian and Ottoman writers both describe soldiers wandering in and seizing the gates.

claims.text: Buda fell on 29 August 1541, fifteen years to the day after Mohács.
claims.note: The date is recorded in Ottoman and Hungarian sources alike.

reigns.hook: Rewind to 1540. John Zápolya's baby son has been elected king against Ferdinand, and the Sultan has promised to protect him.

reigns.tagline: The baby king of eastern Hungary
reigns.reignEnded: Gave up the title at Speyer
reigns.previously: John Zápolya dies, days after his son is born.
paragraphs: John Sigismund was elected king of Hungary as a two-month-old, against the Habsburg Ferdinand I. When the Ottomans took Buda in 1541 they sent him and his mother east to Transylvania.

He ruled there under Ottoman protection for 30 years. In 1570 he gave up the title of king at Speyer and was recognised as the first Prince of Transylvania. He was also the only Unitarian king in history.
reigns.hook: Back to 1564: Ferdinand dies. His son Maximilian, already crowned in Pozsony, inherits the border war, and old Suleiman is planning one last campaign.

reigns.tagline: The year Suleiman died outside a Hungarian fort
reigns.reignEnded: Died at the Diet of Regensburg
reigns.previously: Ferdinand I dies in Vienna, with Hungary still split in three.
paragraphs: Maximilian was crowned at Pozsony in September 1563, the first coronation in the new capital, so the crown passed smoothly when his father died. To the rest of Europe he was Emperor Maximilian II. He was famously relaxed about religion, and Hungary's nobles, many of them Protestant by now, found him a king they could live with.

In 1566 Suleiman marched for the last time. At Szigetvár, Count Miklós Zrínyi held the fort for about a month with a couple of thousand men. In early September, with the walls in ruins, he led his last soldiers out in a charge and died fighting. Suleiman had died in his tent the day before. His ministers kept it secret so the army wouldn't panic.

Maximilian's big imperial army sat near Győr and did almost nothing. Peace in 1568 left the border where it was. In 1570, at Speyer, John Sigismund gave up the title King of Hungary and became Prince of Transylvania, accepting Maximilian as king. It settled the question of the crown, though Transylvania went its own way.

claims.text: Suleiman died in his tent during the siege, and his death was kept secret from the army.
claims.note: Ottoman sources describe how Grand Vizier Sokollu Mehmed hid the death for weeks until the new sultan was secure.

claims.text: Zrínyi left a fuse burning in the castle's powder store, and it blew up as the Turks rushed in.
claims.note: A gunpowder explosion that killed many attackers is reported. That Zrínyi planned it is a later heroic touch.

claims.text: Maximilian refused the Catholic last rites on his deathbed.
claims.note: Witnesses reported it, and Protestants took it as a sign of secret sympathy. What he really believed is still argued over.

reigns.hook: Maximilian dies in 1576. His son Rudolf takes over, a strange, brilliant recluse who will rule Hungary from far-off Prague.

reigns.tagline: The recluse in Prague who lost Hungary to his brother
reigns.previously: Maximilian dies at Regensburg; Rudolf, crowned in 1572, takes over.
paragraphs: Rudolf had been crowned King of Hungary at Pozsony in 1572. Once in charge, he moved his court to Prague and filled it with astrologers, alchemists and art. To Europe he was Emperor Rudolf II; Hungary mostly saw his generals. In 1593 border raids turned into the Long Turkish War, thirteen years of sieges back and forth across the country.

Transylvania's prince Sigismund Báthory changed sides again and again, abdicating and coming back more than once. Unpaid imperial troops plundered the land, and Rudolf's officials pushed the Counter-Reformation hard, seizing churches and putting rich Protestant nobles on trial. In 1604 the Calvinist lord Stephen Bocskai rose in revolt, backed by the hajdús, tough cattle-drovers turned soldiers.

Bocskai won. The Peace of Vienna in 1606 promised religious freedom and made him Prince of Transylvania, and the Peace of Zsitvatorok ended the Turkish war that same year. Rudolf's family decided he was unfit to rule. His brother Matthias marched on Prague with Hungarian backing, and in June 1608 Rudolf handed over Hungary.

claims.text: Rudolf suffered long bouts of deep melancholy and shut himself away from his ministers.
claims.note: Ambassadors' reports from Prague describe it again and again. What his illness really was is guesswork.

claims.text: Bocskai was poisoned by his own chancellor, Mihály Káthay.
claims.note: Káthay was accused after Bocskai's death in December 1606 and killed by angry hajdús. Proof was never shown.

reigns.hook: The Hungarian nobles have made a king. Matthias owes them his crown, and the bill is about to arrive.

reigns.tagline: The brother who paid for Hungary with freedoms
reigns.previously: Rudolf, cornered in Prague, hands Hungary to his brother Matthias.
paragraphs: Matthias had taken Hungary with Hungarian help, and the price came due at once. Before his coronation on 19 November 1608, the Diet made him accept laws on freedom of worship and bring back the palatine, the elected stand-in for the king. He was Matthias II here, since Hungary already had a famous Matthias. In 1612 he also became emperor, where he was plain Matthias.

His reign is best remembered for a scandal. In December 1610 Countess Elizabeth Báthory, a rich widow, was arrested at her castle of Csejte (today Čachtice in Slovakia). Witnesses accused her and her servants of torturing and killing dozens of girls. The servants were executed. She was never tried, but was walled into rooms of the castle and died there in 1614.

In Transylvania, Ottoman backing put Gabriel Bethlen in power in 1613, a clever Calvinist prince who would soon trouble Vienna. Matthias had no children, so the family lined up his hard-line Catholic cousin, Ferdinand of Styria, who was crowned King of Hungary in 1618. Matthias died the next March.

claims.text: Elizabeth Báthory bathed in the blood of virgins to stay young.
claims.note: No witness at the time said so. The story first appears in a Jesuit history printed in 1729, over a century later.

claims.text: Báthory killed hundreds of girls, 650 by one count.
claims.note: The 650 figure came from one witness citing a list nobody produced. Testimony was taken under pressure, and some historians suspect a land grab by her enemies.

claims.text: The 1608 Diet made religious freedom part of Hungarian law.
claims.note: Written into the laws passed before Matthias's coronation.

reigns.hook: Matthias is dead. Ferdinand, a pupil of the Jesuits, takes over just as Bohemia rises in revolt and Bethlen eyes Royal Hungary.

reigns.tagline: The Jesuits' pupil who faced a Calvinist rival
reigns.previously: Matthias II dies in Vienna, childless. His cousin Ferdinand is ready.
paragraphs: Ferdinand had been crowned King of Hungary at Pozsony in July 1618, weeks after the Bohemians threw his officials out of a window in Prague. That started the Thirty Years' War, and Hungary was dragged in at once. Ferdinand, Emperor Ferdinand II, was a fiercely devout Catholic who had already driven Protestant preachers out of his home duchy of Styria.

Gabriel Bethlen, Prince of Transylvania, saw his chance. In 1619 he invaded Royal Hungary and took Pozsony, Holy Crown and all. In August 1620 a diet at Besztercebánya elected him king, but he never had himself crowned. After the Protestants lost at the White Mountain, Bethlen made peace at Nikolsburg at the end of 1621, gave back the crown and kept seven counties for life.

In Hungary the long-term winner was a churchman. Péter Pázmány, born to a Calvinist family, became Archbishop of Esztergom and won noble families back to Rome with sermons, books and sheer persuasion. In 1635 he founded a university at Nagyszombat. It later moved to Buda and grew into Budapest's ELTE.

claims.text: Bethlen was elected King of Hungary in 1620 but was never crowned.
claims.note: The Besztercebánya election is well recorded. Bethlen kept the crown in his hands and the title open for bargaining.
