reigns.tagline: The emperor who finally made peace in Europe
reigns.previously: Ferdinand II dies; his son was crowned at Sopron back in 1625.
paragraphs: Ferdinand had been crowned King of Hungary at Sopron in 1625, aged 17. As Emperor Ferdinand III he took over the Thirty Years' War and badly wanted out of it. Then in 1644 George I Rákóczi, Prince of Transylvania, joined the Swedes and marched into Royal Hungary, saying he had come to protect the Protestants.

The Peace of Linz in 1645 bought Rákóczi off with counties for his lifetime and confirmed freedom of worship. Three years later the Peace of Westphalia ended the war in the rest of Europe. On the Turkish border nothing ended. Raids, ambushes and small sieges went on in the peace years just as they had in the war years.

To make the succession safe, Ferdinand had his eldest son crowned King of Hungary as Ferdinand IV in 1647. The young man died of smallpox in 1654, aged 20. Meanwhile the Croatian-Hungarian lord Miklós Zrínyi, great-grandson of the hero of Szigetvár, fought the Turks on the border and wrote an epic poem about his ancestor's last stand.

claims.text: Zrínyi's The Siege of Sziget, published in 1651, is the first great Hungarian epic poem.
claims.note: The standard view in Hungarian literary history. It is still taught in schools.

claims.text: Rákóczi's 1644 campaign was planned together with Sweden.
claims.note: He made a formal alliance with Sweden and France before marching.

reigns.hook: Ferdinand dies in 1657. His son Leopold, raised for the Church, is king at 16, and the next half-century brings Vienna besieged and Buda set free.

reigns.tagline: Vienna besieged, Buda freed, Hungary in revolt
reigns.previously: Ferdinand III dies. His son Leopold, crowned in 1655, is king at 16.
paragraphs: In 1664 an imperial army beat the Turks at Szentgotthárd. Days later Leopold signed the Peace of Vasvár, letting the sultan keep what he had just won. Hungarians were furious. That November their great hope, the poet-general Miklós Zrínyi, was killed by a wild boar while hunting. Angry nobles around the palatine Ferenc Wesselényi began plotting against Vienna.

The plot was betrayed. In 1671 Péter Zrínyi, the poet's brother, and Ferenc Frangepán were beheaded at Wiener Neustadt, and Leopold ruled Hungary like conquered land. Rebels called kuruc took to the hills, and under Imre Thököly they won most of Upper Hungary. In 1683 the Turks, Thököly's allies, besieged Vienna and were routed.

Then the tide turned. On 2 September 1686 a Christian army retook Buda after 145 years. A grateful Diet in 1687 made the crown hereditary for Habsburg males and gave up the nobles' old right to resist an unjust king. The Peace of Karlowitz in 1699 won back nearly all of Hungary. In 1703 Francis II Rákóczi raised a new kuruc revolt.

claims.text: Zrínyi was murdered on Vienna's orders, and the boar was a cover story.
claims.note: The rumour spread at once. People who were there described a hunting accident, and no evidence of murder has turned up.

claims.text: Buda was retaken on 2 September 1686, after 145 years of Ottoman rule.
claims.note: Recorded in detail by both sides.

claims.text: The sultan recognised Thököly as King of Upper Hungary in 1682.
claims.note: Thököly ruled as an Ottoman vassal and marched with the Turks to Vienna.

reigns.hook: Leopold dies in 1705 with Rákóczi's kuruc raiding almost to the gates of Vienna. His son Joseph has to win the war or make peace.

reigns.tagline: The young king the kuruc tried to dethrone
reigns.previously: Leopold dies with Rákóczi's kuruc rebels raiding near Vienna.
paragraphs: Joseph had been crowned at Pozsony in 1687, aged nine, the first king crowned under the new hereditary law. He was easier-going than his father and wanted a deal. Prince Francis II Rákóczi, grandson of Transylvanian princes and Hungary's richest landowner, was in no mood. His kuruc armies held most of the country, and Transylvania had elected him its prince.

In 1707 the Diet of Ónod went all the way and declared the Habsburgs dethroned. Rákóczi hoped for help from Louis XIV of France and Tsar Peter the Great, but little came. In August 1708 his army broke at Trencsén, and plague and hunger did the rest. Year by year the kuruc lost ground.

Joseph caught smallpox and died in Vienna on 17 April 1711, aged 32. Rákóczi's general Sándor Károlyi had already negotiated terms, and the Peace of Szatmár was signed on 30 April: pardons, the old liberties and an end to the fighting. Rákóczi refused it and went into exile. He ended his days in Rodostó in Turkey.

claims.text: At Ónod, enraged delegates hacked down a county deputy who spoke against the kuruc leadership.
claims.note: The killing of Melchior Rakovszky of Turóc county in 1707 is recorded by Rákóczi himself and others at the diet.

claims.text: The word kuruc comes from the crusaders of the 1514 peasant revolt.
claims.note: One theory traces it to Latin cruciatus, crusader. Others suggest a Turkish origin. Nobody knows for sure.

claims.text: Rákóczi's bones were brought home from Turkey in 1906 and buried at Kassa.
claims.note: His remains were reburied in Kassa (Košice) cathedral, where they still lie.

reigns.hook: Rewind to 1705. The Kuruc rebels have a prince of their own, Francis Rákóczi, and they mean to throw the Habsburgs out of Hungary.

reigns.tagline: The last Habsburg male and his daughter problem
reigns.previously: Joseph I dies of smallpox; the Peace of Szatmár ends Rákóczi's war.
paragraphs: Charles was in Barcelona, fighting to be King of Spain, when his brother died. He came home and was crowned at Pozsony in May 1712. To Europe he was Emperor Charles VI; to the Hungarians, Charles III. He kept the deal made at Szatmár, and a country worn out by nearly two centuries of war settled down at last.

In 1716 Prince Eugene of Savoy smashed the Turks at Petrovaradin and took Temesvár, freeing the Banat, the last Ottoman corner of Hungary. Belgrade fell the next year. The south was half empty after so much fighting, so settlers poured in: German Catholics the Hungarians called Swabians, plus Serbs, Slovaks and Romanians. The map of the south still shows it.

Charles had no living son. His Pragmatic Sanction let a daughter inherit all his lands, and in 1723 the Hungarian Diet accepted it in return for promises to respect Hungary's laws. He lost Belgrade again in 1739. In October 1740 he fell ill after a hunting trip and died within days, the last male Habsburg.

claims.text: Charles died from a dish of poisonous mushrooms.
claims.note: Voltaire wrote that a pot of mushrooms changed the fate of Europe. Doctors at the time were unsure, and some historians suspect a liver illness.

claims.text: The Hungarian Diet accepted the Pragmatic Sanction in 1723.
claims.note: Passed as laws of the 1722–23 Diet at Pozsony.

claims.text: Most of the 'Swabians' did not come from Swabia.
claims.note: Settlers came from many German lands, but Hungarians used the one name for all of them.

reigns.tagline: The 'King' who won over a hall full of Hungarian nobles
reigns.previously: Charles III dies with no son. Everything rides on a paper promise.
paragraphs: The ink on the Pragmatic Sanction meant nothing once her father was dead. Prussia grabbed Silesia, Bavaria and France piled in, and the young queen had an empty treasury and a baby son. She turned to Hungary. On 25 June 1741 she was crowned at Pozsony with the Holy Crown, and since Hungarian law spoke only of kings, she was crowned "King". She rode up the coronation mound and swung the sword to the four corners, like every king before her.

In September 1741 she stood before the Diet and asked for help. The nobles, who had fought her family for two centuries, roared "vitam et sanguinem": our life and our blood. They raised troops, and the hussars helped save her throne. She paid them back carefully. Hungarian nobles kept their freedom from tax, got their own guard at court in Vienna, and Fiume became Hungary's sea port in 1779.

She also leaned on the lords who squeezed their peasants. Her Urbarium of 1767 fixed how much land a serf held and how much labour he owed. She ruled for forty years and died in Vienna in November 1780. Her son Joseph, already emperor and her co-ruler, had been waiting a long time.

claims.text: She held the baby Joseph up in her arms as the nobles shouted "vitam et sanguinem".
claims.note: The famous scene merges two sessions. Contemporary reports put the shout on 11 September 1741 and the baby's appearance at a later sitting that month.

claims.text: The nobles promised their life and blood, "but no oats".
claims.note: A joke added later about stingy nobles; no record from the Diet contains it.

claims.text: She was crowned "King" (rex) of Hungary.
claims.note: The coronation records and her Hungarian title call her rex, as they had Mary in 1382.

reigns.hook: Joseph has big plans and no patience. He has no intention of swearing an oath to Hungary's old laws, so he simply won't be crowned.

reigns.tagline: The reformer who locked the Holy Crown in a museum
reigns.previously: Maria Theresa dies after forty years, still loved in Hungary.
paragraphs: Joseph wanted one tidy, modern state run from Vienna, and Hungary's ancient privileges were in the way. A coronation would mean swearing to uphold them, so he skipped it. Hungarians called him "the king in a hat". In 1784 he had the Holy Crown carted off to Vienna and put in the treasury like an exhibit. That same year German replaced Latin as the language of government.

Some of his changes were bold. His Edict of Toleration of 1781 let Protestants and Orthodox Christians worship openly. In 1784 Romanian peasants in Transylvania rose under Horea, and the revolt was crushed. The next year Joseph abolished "perpetual serfdom", so a peasant could now marry, learn a trade or move away without the lord's say. The nobles, who also faced a census and land survey, were furious and talked of revolt.

By 1789 Joseph was dying, bogged down in a Turkish war and facing rebellion in Belgium. A few weeks before his death he cancelled his Hungarian decrees, keeping only three, toleration and the serf reform among them. The Holy Crown came home to Buda in February 1790 to bonfires and cheering crowds.

claims.text: Hungarians called him "the king in a hat" (kalapos király) because he was never crowned.
claims.note: The nickname is recorded from his own time and is standard in Hungarian histories.

claims.text: On his deathbed he revoked almost all his Hungarian reforms.
claims.note: His rescript of January 1790 withdrew them, keeping the Toleration edict, the serf patent and a decree on parish priests.

claims.text: His epitaph called him a ruler who failed in everything he undertook.
claims.note: Joseph is said to have proposed this wording himself. It is widely quoted, but it is not on his coffin.

reigns.hook: Joseph's brother Leopold rushes from Florence to a monarchy on the brink. The Hungarian nobles are drafting demands, and some are whispering about a foreign king.

reigns.tagline: The fixer who talked Hungary down from the ledge
reigns.previously: Joseph dies, his reforms undone. The Holy Crown comes home.
paragraphs: Leopold had spent 25 years running Tuscany, and he was a far smoother operator than his brother. Hungary's Diet met in 1790 in a fighting mood. Nobles wore Hungarian dress, spoke of a new contract with the king, and a few even sounded out Prussia. Leopold made peace with Prussia and the Turks, then quietly stirred up the kingdom's Serbs and townspeople so the nobles felt less sure of themselves.

Then he gave them what they really wanted. He was crowned at Pozsony on 15 November 1790 and signed a law, Law X, that declared Hungary a free and independent kingdom, to be ruled by its own laws and customs and not like the other Habsburg lands. The nobles went home happy. Leopold kept a close eye on them anyway, through a network of police spies.
He had barely settled things when he fell ill in early 1792 and died within days, aged 44. His 24-year-old son Francis took over, just as revolutionary France was about to go to war.

claims.text: Ignác Martinovics, later the leader of the Hungarian Jacobins, worked as one of Leopold's secret police informers.
claims.note: Reports he wrote for Leopold's police survive; historians differ on how seriously Leopold took him.

claims.text: Leopold was poisoned.
claims.note: Rumours flew because he died so fast. His doctors bled him repeatedly; most historians think illness and the treatment killed him.

reigns.tagline: The emperor who hated change, and the count who forced it
reigns.previously: Leopold dies suddenly after two years of careful deals.
paragraphs: In Vienna he was Emperor Francis II, later Francis I of Austria; in Hungary, King Francis I. He was frightened of revolution and trusted nobody. In 1794 his police uncovered a small Hungarian Jacobin plot led by the former informer Ignác Martinovics. In May 1795 Martinovics and four comrades were beheaded on the Vérmező, the "field of blood" below Buda castle.

The wars with France dragged on for twenty years. In 1809 Napoleon called on the Hungarians to break away and choose their own king. Hardly anyone listened. Instead the nobles turned out their ancient levy, a feudal call to arms, and it was beaten near Győr that June. It was the last time the levy ever fought. After the wars Francis ruled without calling the Diet for thirteen years.

When it finally met in 1825, a young cavalry officer, Count István Széchenyi, stood up and offered a year's income from his estates to found a learned society for the Hungarian language. That became the Hungarian Academy of Sciences. The Reform Era had begun. When Francis died in 1835, his heir was his eldest son, Ferdinand, a kind man who suffered from epilepsy.

claims.text: Széchenyi gave a full year's income to found the Academy of Sciences.
claims.note: The offer at the Diet on 3 November 1825 is well documented, and others quickly matched it.

claims.text: Napoleon's 1809 proclamation asked the Hungarians to gather on the Rákos field and elect a king of their own.
claims.note: The printed appeal of May 1809 survives. It found almost no takers.

reigns.hook: The new king is kind but too ill to rule, so others will govern for him. In Hungary the reformers are getting louder, and a lawyer called Lajos Kossuth is about to be sent to prison.

reigns.tagline: The gentle king who signed away the old order
reigns.previously: Francis dies. Hungary's Reform Era is in full swing.
paragraphs: Emperor Ferdinand I of Austria was Ferdinand V in Hungary, where he had already been crowned in 1830. He suffered from epilepsy and others ruled for him. Hungary, meanwhile, was buzzing. Széchenyi was building the first permanent bridge between Buda and Pest, the Chain Bridge. Kossuth, freed after three years in prison, ran the newspaper Pesti Hírlap from 1841 and became the hero of the reformers.

Then came 1848. On 15 March, with revolution in Paris and Vienna, young radicals in Pest read out the poet Sándor Petőfi's "National Song" ("Rise up, Hungarians!"), and the crowd swept through the city. Within weeks Ferdinand signed the April Laws: serfdom abolished, nobles to pay tax, an elected parliament and Hungary's own government under Count Lajos Batthyány, with Kossuth as finance minister.

Vienna soon regretted it. In September the Croatian governor Josip Jelačić invaded Hungary with the court's blessing, and was turned back at Pákozd. Vienna itself rose in October and was crushed. The court decided the gentle Ferdinand had to go. On 2 December 1848 at Olmütz he gave up his thrones to his 18-year-old nephew.

claims.text: Ferdinand's last words as emperor to his nephew were "Be good, God will protect you".
claims.note: Reported by witnesses at Olmütz, but the wording varies from account to account.

claims.text: Petőfi recited the National Song on the steps of the National Museum on 15 March.
claims.note: It is the famous image, but contemporary accounts suggest he read it at several spots that day, and the museum moment may be less certain than the legend.

claims.text: Told he could not have apricot dumplings, he snapped: "I'm the emperor and I want dumplings!"
claims.note: A popular Viennese anecdote told to mock him; it has no reliable contemporary source.

reigns.title: Lajos Kossuth
reigns.tagline: The lawyer who declared Hungary free of the Habsburgs
reigns.previously: Ferdinand abdicates. Hungary refuses to accept his teenage nephew.
paragraphs: Kossuth was a small-town lawyer with a gift for words. By late 1848 he led the committee running Hungary's defence, printing his own banknotes to pay an army. Austrian troops took Pest in January 1849, and the government fled to Debrecen. Then the Hungarians struck back. On 14 April 1849, in Debrecen's great Protestant church, Kossuth declared the Habsburgs deposed. He was named Governor-President.

General Artúr Görgei's spring campaign drove the Austrians back, and Buda castle fell to the Hungarians on 21 May. But Franz Joseph asked Russia for help, and in June a huge Russian army crossed the mountains. Petőfi vanished at the battle of Segesvár on 31 July. On 11 August Kossuth handed power to Görgei and fled to Ottoman territory. Two days later Görgei surrendered to the Russians at Világos.

The revenge was brutal. On 6 October 1849, thirteen Hungarian generals were executed at Arad, and in Pest the former prime minister Batthyány was shot the same day. Kossuth lived on in exile for 45 years. He toured Britain and America in 1851 and 1852, where huge crowds cheered him. He died in Turin in 1894 and was buried in Budapest.

claims.text: Hungarians don't clink beer glasses because Austrian officers did so to celebrate the executions at Arad.
claims.note: There is no evidence of such toasts at Arad. The custom is real, but the story behind it was attached later.

claims.text: Petőfi was killed at Segesvár.
claims.note: His body was never found. Theories that he was taken to Siberia as a prisoner have been widely rejected by historians.

claims.text: Thirteen generals were executed at Arad on 6 October 1849.
claims.note: Court-martial records and many witnesses agree; Hungary still marks the day as a national day of mourning.

reigns.hook: Hungary's dream lies broken, and the young emperor's generals are hanging rebels. Franz Joseph will rule for 67 more years. Can Hungary ever forgive him?

reigns.tagline: From hangman of Hungary to its crowned king
reigns.previously: Kossuth flees. Thirteen generals are executed at Arad.
paragraphs: Franz Joseph began as Hungary's enemy. General Haynau, "the hyena of Brescia", ran the reprisals, and for over a decade Hungary was governed straight from Vienna by officials Hungarians mocked as "Bach hussars". Then Austria lost two wars, to France and Piedmont in 1859 and to Prussia in 1866. The emperor needed Hungary on side, and the lawyer Ferenc Deák was ready to deal.

The Compromise of 1867 split the empire in two: Austria-Hungary, with one ruler, one army and one foreign policy, but its own parliament in Budapest. On 8 June 1867 Franz Joseph was crowned in Buda's Matthias Church, with Franz Liszt's Coronation Mass. Beside him was Queen Elisabeth, Sisi, who had learned Hungarian and adored the country. The nation gave the couple Gödöllő palace.

Budapest, formed in 1873, boomed. In 1896 it celebrated a thousand years since the Magyars arrived, with the start of Heroes' Square and the continent's first underground railway. Private sorrows piled up: his son Rudolf died at Mayerling in 1889, Sisi was stabbed in Geneva in 1898. In 1914 he went to war with Serbia. He died in 1916, aged 86, before he could see the end.

claims.text: Sisi pushed for the Compromise and favoured Count Gyula Andrássy, its Hungarian architect.
claims.note: Her sympathy for Hungary is well attested. How far she shaped policy, and the romance rumours with Andrássy, are debated.

claims.text: Budapest's 1896 metro line was the first underground railway on the European continent.
claims.note: Opened in May 1896 for the millennium; only London's was older.

reigns.hook: The old emperor is gone mid-war. His heir is his 29-year-old great-nephew Charles, who wants peace and must be crowned in Budapest at once.

reigns.previously: Franz Joseph dies after 68 years, with the war still raging.
paragraphs: Emperor Charles I of Austria was Charles IV in Hungary. Prime Minister István Tisza insisted he be crowned fast, to bind him to Hungary's constitution. On 30 December 1916 the Holy Crown was placed on his head in the Matthias Church in Budapest, with his wife Zita and their small son Otto beside him. Nobody watching knew it was the last Hungarian coronation.

Charles wanted out of the war. In 1917 he secretly sent peace feelers to France through Zita's brother Sixtus, and when the letters leaked the next year, Germany was outraged and he was humiliated. By October 1918 the army was falling apart. On 31 October soldiers shot Tisza dead in his villa. In Budapest crowds wore asters in their caps, and the liberal Count Mihály Károlyi took power in the "Aster Revolution".
On 13 November 1918, at his hunting lodge at Eckartsau, Charles signed a statement giving up any part in governing Hungary. He was careful never to use the word abdicate.

claims.text: Charles never abdicated as King of Hungary.
claims.note: The Eckartsau declaration only withdrew him from state affairs; he insisted on this distinction for the rest of his life.

claims.text: Charles was beatified by the Catholic Church in 2004.
claims.note: Pope John Paul II beatified him in Rome on 3 October 2004.

reigns.hook: Charles steps aside. In Budapest Count Mihály Károlyi, the liberal hero of the Aster Revolution, proclaims a republic. But the Allies want Hungarian land, and the communists are getting ready.

reigns.title: Mihály Károlyi
reigns.tagline: The Red Count who gave his own land away
reigns.previously: Charles steps back from Hungarian affairs, but he never abdicates.
paragraphs: Count Mihály Károlyi was born into one of the richest families in Hungary, yet he spent the war calling for peace and attacking the alliance with Germany. When the army fell apart in October 1918, Budapest crowds stuck asters in their caps, and on 31 October he was made prime minister. On 16 November Hungary was proclaimed a republic. From here on, the deck follows whoever really held power.

The war was lost, and the neighbours knew it. Czech, Serb and Romanian troops moved into lands Hungary had ruled for centuries, and the Allies kept drawing new lines on the map. In January 1919 Károlyi became provisional president. In February he started sharing out his own estate at Kápolna among the farm workers. People called him the Red Count.

On 20 March 1919 the French Lieutenant-Colonel Fernand Vix delivered a note ordering Hungarian troops to pull back even further. Károlyi's government could neither accept it nor fight it. The next day power passed to the Social Democrats and the Communists. Károlyi soon left the country and spent most of the rest of his life in exile.

claims.text: Károlyi never signed the resignation that handed power to the Communists.
claims.note: A proclamation in his name announced the handover on 21 March 1919. In exile he insisted it went out without his signature; historians still argue over how far he agreed to it.

claims.text: Károlyi gave his own estate away to farm workers.
claims.note: In February 1919 he began dividing his estate at Kápolna. It was a gesture; the wider land reform barely started before his government fell.

reigns.hook: In a Budapest prison cell sits Béla Kun, a journalist who turned Bolshevik as a prisoner of war in Russia. Within hours he will be running the country, counting on Lenin's Red Army to come to his aid.

reigns.title: Béla Kun
reigns.tagline: 133 days of Soviet Hungary
reigns.cameToPower: Freed from prison to take power
reigns.previously: The Allies demand yet more land, and Károlyi's government gives up.
paragraphs: Béla Kun was a journalist from Transylvania who became a Bolshevik as a prisoner of war in Russia. He founded the Hungarian Communist Party in November 1918 and was arrested in February 1919. On 21 March the Social Democrats came to the prison to make a deal. The two parties merged, and that evening the Hungarian Soviet Republic was proclaimed. Sándor Garbai chaired its council, but Kun, the commissar for foreign affairs, ran it.

The new regime nationalised factories, banks, shops and the big estates. It kept the estates as state farms instead of handing them to the peasants, and the countryside turned against it. Its Red Army did better than anyone expected, pushing deep into Slovakia, then pulled back when the Allies promised that the Romanians would withdraw. They never did. Behind the lines Tibor Szamuely and his Lenin Boys hunted down enemies and hanged peasant rebels.

In late July the Red Army attacked across the Tisza, and the Romanians broke through. On 1 August Kun resigned and escaped to Austria. In Soviet Russia he headed the Bolshevik committee in Crimea in 1920–21, which carried out mass shootings of surrendered White soldiers and civilians. He then worked for the Communist International. In Stalin's purges he was arrested, and in 1938 he was shot.

claims.text: The Red Terror killed around 500 to 600 people.
claims.note: Estimates run from a few hundred to about 600. The White Terror that followed is generally thought to have killed more.

claims.text: Szamuely toured the country in an armoured train ordering executions.
claims.note: His train and its squad are described in court records and memoirs. Szamuely died fleeing to Austria in August 1919.

claims.text: Kun was shot in the Soviet Union in 1938.
claims.note: Arrested in June 1937. When Moscow rehabilitated him in 1956 it gave a false death date in 1939; only in 1989 did Soviet officials admit he was shot on 29 August 1938.

reigns.hook: Kun's train heads for Austria. Left holding Budapest is Gyula Peidl, a Social Democrat trade unionist, with the Romanian army almost at the gates.

reigns.title: Gyula Peidl
reigns.tagline: Six days in charge, then the Romanians marched in
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Social Democrat who took over from Kun
reigns.previously: Kun resigns and flees to Austria. The Romanians are closing in.
paragraphs: Gyula Peidl was a veteran trade-union leader who had kept his distance from the Communists. On 1 August 1919 the Social Democrats put him at the head of what Hungarians nicknamed the trade-union government. Its plan was simple: end the dictatorship, undo the nationalisations and persuade the Allies it was safe to talk to.

There was no time. Romanian troops marched into Budapest on 4 August, and the right was plotting openly. On 6 August a small group of armed men led by István Friedrich turned up at the cabinet meeting and told the ministers to resign. They did. Peidl's government had lasted six days.

claims.text: Friedrich's coup took only a handful of armed men.
claims.note: Accounts agree the ministers were simply ordered out; the Romanian troops in the city did nothing to stop it.

claims.text: Peidl's cabinet was called the trade-union government.
claims.note: Most of its ministers came from the unions, and Hungarian historians still use the name.

reigns.hook: The man in charge now is István Friedrich, a factory owner with no mandate at all. And he has brought a Habsburg archduke back to sit at the top of the state.

reigns.title: István Friedrich
reigns.tagline: The factory owner who took power in one night
reigns.cameToPower: Coup backed by a Habsburg archduke
reigns.previously: Peidl's trade-union government lasts six days. Romania holds Budapest.
paragraphs: István Friedrich was an engineer who owned a machine factory and had served in Károlyi's government. After the coup of 6 August 1919, Archduke Joseph August, a Habsburg, took charge as head of state and named Friedrich prime minister. The Allies were having none of it. They would not accept a Habsburg back in power, and on 23 August the archduke had to step down.

Meanwhile the Romanian army stripped the country, loading machines, railway wagons and livestock onto trains bound for Romania. In the countryside officers' squads of the White Terror beat, hanged and shot suspected communists and, above all, Jews. Friedrich's government did little to stop them.

On 16 November 1919, two days after the Romanians left the capital, Admiral Miklós Horthy rode into Budapest on a white horse at the head of his National Army. The Allied envoy Sir George Clerk made it plain he would only deal with a government that took in all the main parties. On 24 November Friedrich gave way.

claims.text: Horthy entered Budapest on a white horse.
claims.note: It was staged as a show and caught by photographers and newsreel cameras on 16 November 1919, along with his speech about the sinful city.

claims.text: The Romanian army carried off huge amounts of Hungarian property.
claims.note: Hungarian and Allied reports at the time listed the requisitions; the totals each side gave differed widely.

claims.text: Friedrich died in a communist prison.
claims.note: He was jailed after the communist takeover and died in Vác prison in November 1951.

reigns.hook: Clerk gets his coalition. At its head is Károly Huszár, a Christian Nationalist, who must hold Hungary's first secret-ballot election and face the peace terms.

reigns.title: Károly Huszár
reigns.tagline: The stopgap premier who brought in the secret ballot
reigns.previously: Horthy rides into Budapest. The Allies demand a broader government.
paragraphs: Károly Huszár was a Christian Nationalist politician whom the Allies' envoy Sir George Clerk could accept. His cabinet took in the Smallholders, the Liberals and the Social Democrats, and on that basis the Allies recognised it. As prime minister he was also acting head of state.

In January 1920 Hungary held its first election with a secret ballot, and women voted too. The Social Democrats quit the government and boycotted the vote in protest at the White Terror, so the Smallholders and the Christian parties took almost all the seats. That same month Count Albert Apponyi's delegation was handed the peace terms in Paris. Hungary was to lose about two thirds of its territory.

The new parliament declared that Hungary was still a kingdom, with the king kept out. On 1 March 1920, with Horthy's officers in and around the building, it elected the admiral regent. Huszár stayed on as prime minister for another two weeks.

claims.text: The 1920 election was Hungary's first with a secret ballot and women voting.
claims.note: Held in January 1920; open voting returned in the countryside in 1922.

claims.text: Armed officers surrounded parliament on the day Horthy was elected.
claims.note: Contemporaries and historians such as Romsics and Sakmyster describe his troops in and around the building during the vote.

reigns.hook: The regent is Miklós Horthy, an admiral whose navy no longer exists. Charles IV is barred from returning, and the peace treaty is waiting to be signed.

reigns.title: Miklós Horthy
reigns.tagline: Regent of a kingdom that had no king
reigns.previously: Huszár's newly elected parliament votes the admiral in as regent.
paragraphs: Horthy had been the last commander of the Austro-Hungarian navy. On 4 June 1920 the Treaty of Trianon took about two thirds of Hungary's territory, and millions of Hungarians found themselves in Czechoslovakia, Romania and Yugoslavia. Twice in 1921 Charles IV came back to claim his throne, and twice Horthy refused to step aside. Already in 1920 a law, the numerus clausus, had capped the number of Jewish students at universities.

Winning back the lost lands became the aim of Horthy's Hungary, and Nazi Germany offered the means. Anti-Jewish laws in 1938, 1939 and 1941 pushed Jews out of jobs and banned their marriages with non-Jews. The Vienna Awards of 1938 and 1940 returned parts of Slovakia and Transylvania. In April 1941 Prime Minister Pál Teleki shot himself rather than join the attack on Yugoslavia. Hungary joined it anyway, and in June 1941 went to war with the Soviet Union.

In January 1943 the Hungarian Second Army was destroyed on the Don. When Horthy looked for a way out, Germany occupied Hungary on 19 March 1944. Between May and July about 437,000 Jews were deported, rounded up by Hungarian gendarmes, and most were murdered at Auschwitz. Horthy halted the deportations in July. On 15 October he announced on the radio that Hungary was leaving the war. The Germans kidnapped his son and forced him out.

claims.text: Hungary was a kingdom without a king, ruled by an admiral without a sea.
claims.note: Both halves are true: the throne stayed empty, and Trianon left Hungary landlocked. The quip itself is old and has no known author.

claims.text: Teleki left a note saying Hungary had broken its word.
claims.note: His farewell letter to Horthy said the country had become a breaker of its word, after a friendship treaty with Yugoslavia signed only months before.

claims.text: Horthy stopped the deportations in July 1944.
claims.note: He ordered a halt in early July, under Allied, neutral and papal pressure. By then the Jews outside Budapest had almost all been deported.

reigns.hook: Horthy is taken to Germany under guard. The Germans hand power to Ferenc Szálasi, leader of the Arrow Cross, and the Jews still living in Budapest are in mortal danger.

reigns.title: Ferenc Szálasi
reigns.tagline: The Arrow Cross leader installed by the Germans
reigns.reignEnded: Fled as the Red Army advanced
reigns.previously: Horthy tries to quit the war. The Germans kidnap his son and oust him.
paragraphs: Ferenc Szálasi was a former army officer who led the Arrow Cross, Hungary's fascist party. On 16 October 1944 the Germans put him in charge, and he styled himself Leader of the Nation. In November the Arrow Cross and Adolf Eichmann's men drove tens of thousands of Budapest's Jews on foot towards the Austrian border to dig defences. Many died on the road from cold, hunger and shooting.

In Budapest armed Arrow Cross gangs ruled the streets. They dragged Jews from the ghetto and from protected houses, lined them up on the Danube bank, made them take off their shoes and shot them into the river. Foreign diplomats tried to save whoever they could. The Swede Raoul Wallenberg and the Swiss Carl Lutz issued protective papers and ran safe houses that sheltered tens of thousands.

Soviet troops surrounded Budapest at Christmas 1944. The siege lasted until 13 February 1945 and left the city in ruins. Szálasi had already fled west. The last German troops left Hungary in early April. Szálasi was caught in Austria, sent back, tried by a People's Court and hanged in Budapest in March 1946.

claims.text: The Shoes on the Danube Bank memorial marks where the Arrow Cross shot Jews into the river.
claims.note: Sixty pairs of iron shoes by Can Togay and Gyula Pauer were set on the Pest embankment in 2005. Survivor testimony and trial records document the killings.

claims.text: Raoul Wallenberg died in a Soviet prison in 1947.
claims.note: Soviet troops detained him in January 1945. Moscow later said he died of a heart attack in 1947; Sweden only formally declared him dead in 2016.

claims.text: Communist Hungary celebrated 4 April as Liberation Day.
claims.note: The date of the last German withdrawal was a national holiday until 1989.

reigns.hook: The Germans are gone and the Red Army stays. A provisional government sits in the ruins, led by General Béla Miklós, who went over to the Soviets in 1944. The Communists have Moscow behind them.

reigns.title: Béla Miklós
reigns.tagline: The general who changed sides and ran the ruins
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Horthy general who joined the Soviets
reigns.previously: Budapest lies in ruins and the last German troops have left Hungary.
paragraphs: Béla Miklós of Dálnok had headed Horthy's military office. In October 1944, commanding the First Army in the Carpathians, he crossed over to the Soviets after Horthy's failed attempt to leave the war. On 22 December 1944, in Soviet-held Debrecen, a hastily gathered Provisional National Assembly made him prime minister of a Provisional National Government.

His government declared war on Germany and signed an armistice in Moscow in January 1945. In spring it moved to Budapest, where the siege had left the bridges in the river and whole districts in rubble. In March 1945 a sweeping land reform broke up the great estates and handed land to hundreds of thousands of peasants.

Real power sat with the Allied Control Commission, chaired by the Soviet Marshal Kliment Voroshilov. The Communists, back from Moscow with Mátyás Rákosi, were few but well placed. On 4 November 1945 Hungarians voted freely, and the Smallholders won about 57 per cent. Miklós made way for the winners.

claims.text: The Smallholders won about 57 per cent in November 1945.
claims.note: Official results of 4 November 1945; the Communists and the Social Democrats each got about 17 per cent.

claims.text: Miklós went over to the Red Army in October 1944.
claims.note: He crossed the lines days after Horthy's failed armistice bid of 15 October; few of his troops followed him.

reigns.title: Zoltán Tildy
reigns.tagline: The pastor who won a majority and still had to share
reigns.previously: The Smallholders win a free election with about 57 per cent.
paragraphs: Zoltán Tildy was a Reformed Church pastor and a founder of the Independent Smallholders' Party, the party of farmers and the small-town middle class. In November 1945 it won an outright majority. Marshal Voroshilov told the party leaders they had to govern in a grand coalition anyway, and the Communists got the Interior Ministry, which ran the police.

Tildy took office on 15 November 1945 at the head of a ruined country. Prices were climbing faster every week as the pengő collapsed. In January 1946 the expulsion of Hungary's ethnic Germans began, with trains carrying them to the American zone of Germany.

On 1 February 1946 parliament abolished the kingdom and proclaimed a republic, and Tildy was elected its president. He handed the premiership to his party colleague Ferenc Nagy. In 1948 he was forced to resign after his son-in-law was arrested and accused of spying. In 1956 he joined Imre Nagy's government and went to prison for it.

claims.text: Voroshilov forced the winning Smallholders into a coalition with the Communists.
claims.note: Minutes and memoirs agree the Soviet marshal insisted on it and on a Communist interior minister.

claims.text: Tildy was forced out as president over his son-in-law's arrest.
claims.note: His son-in-law Viktor Csornoky was tried and executed in 1948; Tildy resigned that summer and was put under house arrest.

reigns.title: Ferenc Nagy
reigns.tagline: The farmer premier who swapped his job for his son
reigns.previously: Hungary becomes a republic, and Tildy moves up to president.
paragraphs: Ferenc Nagy was a peasant farmer from Baranya county who had built up the Smallholders' farmers' movement. He became prime minister on 4 February 1946, just as the pengő sank into the worst hyperinflation ever recorded. By July prices were doubling about every 15 hours. On 1 August 1946 the forint replaced it, and the new money held.

The Communist leader Mátyás Rákosi was cutting the Smallholders down one slice at a time, forcing out group after group of their deputies as reactionaries. In February 1947 the Soviet authorities arrested Béla Kovács, the party's general secretary, and took him to the Soviet Union.

In May 1947 Nagy went on holiday to Switzerland. While he was away, the Communists announced that Kovács had named him in a plot. The message from Budapest was blunt: resign and stay abroad, and your young son will be sent out to you. Nagy resigned on 31 May, the boy was handed over at the border, and the family settled in the United States.

claims.text: Nagy resigned in exchange for his son being sent out to him.
claims.note: Nagy told the story in his memoirs, and it was reported at the time; the boy was handed over at the Swiss border in early June 1947.

claims.text: Rákosi called his method salami tactics.
claims.note: The phrase is tied to Rákosi, who later boasted of the method. Who first said it is less clear; some credit his opponents.

claims.text: The pengő hyperinflation was the worst ever recorded.
claims.note: Economists' tables, such as Steve Hanke's, put July 1946 at the top, ahead of Zimbabwe and Weimar Germany.

reigns.title: Lajos Dinnyés
reigns.tagline: The pliant premier of the blue-ballot election
reigns.previously: Ferenc Nagy resigns from exile in return for his son.
paragraphs: Lajos Dinnyés was a Smallholder deputy whom the Communists judged harmless, and they were right. He became prime minister on 31 May 1947, and a new election was called for 31 August.

It became known as the blue-ballot election. Blue slips meant for voters away from home let Communist squads vote again and again in district after district, while many opponents found themselves struck off the rolls. The Communists came first with about 22 per cent, and the Smallholders collapsed.

Then the opposition parties were broken up one by one, and their leaders fled abroad or went to prison. The banks were nationalised, and in March 1948 every firm with more than 100 workers was taken by the state. On 12 June 1948 the Social Democrats were merged into the Communists. Dinnyés stayed prime minister until December, but the party now ruled.

claims.text: The 1947 election was rigged with blue ballots.
claims.note: Blue absentee slips let Communist squads vote many times. The fraud was exposed at the time.

claims.text: The Communists came first with about 22 per cent in 1947.
claims.note: Official results of 31 August 1947; even with the fraud, they were far short of a majority on their own.

reigns.title: Mátyás Rákosi
reigns.tagline: The bald dictator who copied Stalin to the letter
reigns.cameToPower: Head of the merged ruling party
reigns.previously: The Communists swallow the Social Democrats. One party now rules.
paragraphs: Rákosi spent 15 years in Hungarian prisons until, in 1940, Moscow got him out in exchange for flags captured from Hungarian rebels in 1849. Now he built Stalin's system in miniature. A new constitution made Hungary a People's Republic on 20 August 1949. Factories, shops and then farms were taken by the state. His portrait hung everywhere, and his 60th birthday in 1952 was celebrated like a royal jubilee.

The ÁVH secret police filled the prisons. In 1949 the former interior minister László Rajk, a loyal Communist, was tortured into confessing to absurd plots and hanged. In 1951 thousands of 'class enemies' were deported from Budapest to the countryside. Hungarians found joy in football: in November 1953 the Golden Team beat England 6–3 at Wembley.

After Stalin died, Moscow made Imre Nagy prime minister in 1953. He freed prisoners and eased the squeeze on peasants. Rákosi fought back and had Nagy thrown out in 1955. But in 1956 Khrushchev denounced Stalin, and on 18 July Moscow removed Rákosi. He left for the Soviet Union and never came back.

claims.text: Rákosi was hailed as Stalin's best Hungarian pupil.
claims.note: The phrase belongs to his own cult and is often put in his mouth. Whether he coined it himself is not well documented.

claims.text: Rákosi was swapped for the flags of 1849.
claims.note: In 1940 the Soviet Union returned Hungarian revolutionary flags taken by the Russian army in 1849, and Hungary let Rákosi go to Moscow.

claims.text: The 6–3 win was England's first home defeat by a team from outside the British Isles.

reigns.title: Imre Nagy
reigns.tagline: The communist premier who sided with the revolution
reigns.cameToPower: Named PM as the uprising began
reigns.previously: Gerő's hard-line speech turns a student march into a revolution.
paragraphs: On 23 October 1956 students marched through Budapest with a list of demands. By evening a crowd had pulled down the giant Stalin statue, and shooting broke out at the radio building. Overnight the party made Imre Nagy prime minister again, hoping his popularity would calm things. Soviet tanks were already in the streets, and young fighters met them with rifles and petrol bombs.

Nagy moved, step by step, towards the people. On 28 October he declared a ceasefire, and Soviet troops pulled out of Budapest. He brought other parties back into government. On 1 November, as fresh Soviet troops crossed the border, he announced that Hungary was leaving the Warsaw Pact and would be neutral.

At dawn on 4 November the Soviet army attacked. Nagy's radio appeal said the government was at its post. Within days the fighting was over. About 2,500 Hungarians were killed and some 200,000 fled abroad. Nagy took refuge in the Yugoslav embassy, was seized when he left it, tried in secret and hanged on 16 June 1958.

reigns.title: János Kádár
reigns.tagline: The man who crushed 1956, then bought the peace
reigns.reignEnded: Pushed aside at a party conference
reigns.previously: Soviet tanks crush the revolution. Nagy hides in the Yugoslav embassy.
paragraphs: Kádár was born in Fiume to a poor single mother and trained as a typewriter mechanic. An underground Communist, he rose high after 1945, then was jailed and tortured under Rákosi. In November 1956 he came back to Budapest behind Soviet tanks. The reprisals were harsh. Many thousands were jailed, and about 230 people, Nagy among them, were executed for their part in the revolution.

Then he changed course. In 1961 he turned the old Stalinist slogan inside out: whoever is not against us is with us. Political prisoners were amnestied in 1963. In 1968 the New Economic Mechanism let firms chase profits, and private plots and weekend cottages flourished. Hungarians got fuller shops and more chances to travel than most of the bloc. The same year Hungarian troops joined the invasion of Czechoslovakia.

The comfort was bought on credit. Western loans piled up, and by the 1980s the economy was stalling. In May 1988 the party pushed the old man aside. He died on 6 July 1989, the very day the Supreme Court cleared Imre Nagy.

claims.text: Kádár's Hungary was 'the happiest barracks' in the Soviet bloc.
claims.note: A popular quip in the West and in Hungary itself. It sums up the mood of the 1970s and was never meant as a measurement.

claims.text: Kádár reversed Rákosi's slogan: who is not against us is with us.
claims.note: He said it in a speech in December 1961; it became the motto of his softer rule.

claims.text: Kádár died on the day Nagy was rehabilitated.
claims.note: Hungary's Supreme Court annulled Nagy's sentence on 6 July 1989; Kádár died the same day.

reigns.title: Károly Grósz
reigns.tagline: The hard-headed reformer who ran out of time
reigns.previously: After more than 30 years, the party pushes Kádár aside.
paragraphs: Károly Grósz was a career party official from Miskolc who became prime minister in June 1987. At a party conference on 22 May 1988 he replaced the ageing János Kádár as general secretary, and most of Kádár's old guard went out with him. Grósz wanted a market economy, but with the party firmly in charge.

He let new groups organise, and Hungarians could now travel to the West more freely than anyone else in the bloc. In August 1988 he met Romania's dictator Nicolae Ceaușescu at Arad to plead for the Hungarians of Transylvania and came home with nothing. On 24 November he handed the premiership to the young economist Miklós Németh, keeping the party for himself.

It was a bad trade. Days later he warned party members of a coming white terror, and he began to look out of step. The reformers around Németh and Imre Pozsgay drove events from then on. From June 1989 Grósz had to share the leadership, and in October 1989 the party voted itself out of existence.

claims.text: Grósz warned of a white terror in late 1988.
claims.note: He used the phrase in a speech to Budapest party activists at the end of November 1988; it was widely mocked.

claims.text: The Arad meeting with Ceaușescu achieved nothing.
claims.note: The talks of 28 August 1988 brought no concessions for Romania's Hungarians and were seen at home as a humiliation.

reigns.title: Miklós Németh
reigns.tagline: The prime minister who opened the Iron Curtain
reigns.previously: Grósz keeps the party, but gives the government to Németh.
paragraphs: Miklós Németh was an economist who had studied at Harvard and worked in the party's economics department. He became prime minister on 24 November 1988 and decided the state could no longer afford to keep the border fence with Austria in repair. On 2 May 1989 crews began to take it down. On 27 June foreign ministers Gyula Horn and Alois Mock cut a stretch of it for the cameras.

Meanwhile the party sat down with the opposition at the Round Table Talks to agree the rules for free elections. On 16 June a vast crowd in Heroes' Square reburied Imre Nagy. At the Pan-European Picnic near Sopron on 19 August hundreds of East Germans ran across into Austria, and on 11 September Hungary opened its border to every East German who wanted to leave.

In October the ruling party turned itself into the Hungarian Socialist Party, and on 23 October 1989, the anniversary of 1956, the Republic of Hungary was proclaimed. Hungarians voted freely in March and April 1990, and the Democratic Forum came first. On 23 May Németh handed over to József Antall. He later served as a vice-president of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development.

claims.text: Work on removing the border fence began on 2 May 1989.

claims.note: Tens of thousands crossed to Austria in the following weeks, two months before the Berlin Wall fell.

reigns.tagline: The museum director who steered Hungary out of the East
reigns.previously: Round Table deals done; Hungary holds its first free vote since 1945.
paragraphs: József Antall was a historian with a calm voice and very old-fashioned manners. After 1956 he was banned from teaching for his part in the revolution, and he spent the quiet years running the Semmelweis museum of medical history in Budapest. In 1989 he became leader of the Hungarian Democratic Forum, the MDF, and in spring 1990 it came first in Hungary's first free election in more than forty years.

He built a centre-right coalition with the Smallholders and the Christian Democrats, and did a deal with the liberal opposition: their man Árpád Göncz became president. Then reality hit. Prices soared, factories closed, and when fuel prices jumped in October 1990 taxi drivers blockaded the bridges of Budapest for three days. Compensation laws handed out vouchers to people whose property the communists had taken.

The big prize came on 19 June 1991, when the last Soviet troops left Hungary after 47 years. The Warsaw Pact was wound up that summer. But Antall was ill with cancer, and he died in office in December 1993. His interior minister, Péter Boross, held the job until the 1994 election.

claims.text: Antall said he wanted to be prime minister, in spirit, of fifteen million Hungarians.
claims.note: He said it at an MDF meeting in 1990, counting the Hungarians living in neighbouring countries. Hungary's neighbours read it as a threat; Antall said he meant no change of borders.

claims.text: The last Soviet soldiers left Hungary on 19 June 1991.

reigns.tagline: The Iron Curtain cutter who came back to win
reigns.previously: Antall dies in office; Péter Boross keeps the seat warm until 1994.
paragraphs: Gyula Horn was the old regime's last foreign minister, the man who snipped the border fence with Austria's Alois Mock for the cameras in June 1989. In 1994 his Socialists, the renamed communist party, won an absolute majority of seats. Horn still brought in the liberal Free Democrats, giving his government more than two thirds of parliament.

The money had run out. In March 1995 his finance minister Lajos Bokros announced a brutal package: a devalued forint, welfare cuts and new university fees. It was hugely unpopular, but it steadied the economy. Horn sold off big state firms, including the gas and power companies, to foreign buyers, and signed treaties with Slovakia and Romania on their Hungarian minorities.

Hungary was invited to join NATO in 1997, and voters backed it in a referendum that November. In 1998 Horn's party won the most list votes but fewer seats than Fidesz, and he was out. He died in 2013.

reigns.tagline: A 35-year-old takes the top job

reigns.previously: Horn's Socialists win more list votes in 1998, but Fidesz more seats.
paragraphs: Viktor Orbán made his name on 16 June 1989, at the reburial of Imre Nagy, when he told a huge crowd in Heroes' Square that Soviet troops should leave. He had co-founded Fidesz, the Alliance of Young Democrats, in 1988 as a student. After the 1994 defeat he steered the party from youthful liberalism to the right, and in 1998 he became prime minister at 35.

He governed with the Smallholders and the MDF. On 12 March 1999 Hungary joined NATO. For the millennium, the Holy Crown of St Stephen was moved from the National Museum to the Parliament building. A Status Law gave benefits to Hungarians living in neighbouring countries, which angered Romania and Slovakia.
In 2002 the race was tight, and the Socialists and Free Democrats won by a handful of seats. Orbán went into opposition, but not quietly.

paragraphs: Péter Medgyessy was a finance man: finance minister under the communists in the late 1980s, then a banker, then finance minister again under Horn. The Socialists made him their candidate in 2002, and he won. He came in with a '100-day programme' of handouts, including a 50 per cent pay rise for public-sector workers and more money for pensioners. It was popular, and very expensive.

Weeks later the newspaper Magyar Nemzet revealed that he had worked for communist-era counter-intelligence under the code name D-209. He admitted it and stayed on. In April 2003 Hungarians voted yes to joining the European Union, and on 1 May 2004 Hungary became a member. That summer Medgyessy tried to sack ministers, his Free Democrat partners refused, and he resigned.

reigns.tagline: He told the truth in private. Then it leaked.
reigns.previously: Medgyessy resigns after a fight with his coalition partners.
paragraphs: Ferenc Gyurcsány ran the communist youth league in his twenties, then made a fortune in business after 1990. He was sports minister when the Socialists chose him to replace Medgyessy. Young and slick, he did what no Hungarian government had done since 1990: in April 2006 his coalition won re-election.

Then, in September 2006, a recording leaked of a closed-door speech he had given to his party at Balatonőszöd that May. He swore, admitted the government had lied to win, and demanded tough reforms. Protesters stormed the state television building. On 23 October, the 50th anniversary of 1956, rioters clashed with police in Budapest and even got an old Soviet tank from a 1956 display moving.

He survived, barely. Voters threw out his doctor's-visit and tuition fees in a 2008 referendum, his coalition broke up, and the global crash hit Hungary hard. In October 2008 Hungary took a rescue loan of about $25 billion from the IMF, the EU and the World Bank. In March 2009 Gyurcsány said he would step down.

His medicine was bitter. He cut the extra 13th-month pension and public-sector bonus, raised VAT from 20 to 25 per cent, and began raising the retirement age to 65. Markets calmed and Hungary avoided default. Voters were in no mood to thank anyone. The far-right Jobbik party, with its uniformed Hungarian Guard, won nearly 15 per cent in the 2009 European election.
In April 2010 Fidesz won more than two thirds of the seats in parliament. The Socialists collapsed, and Jobbik came third.

paragraphs: Back in power, Orbán moved fast. In 2011 his two-thirds majority passed a new constitution, the Fundamental Law, and parliament shrank to 199 seats. New media and election rules followed. In 2014, 2018 and 2022 Fidesz won two thirds again. In a 2014 speech in Romania he said he was building an 'illiberal state'.

In 2015, as refugees crossed the Balkans, he put up a razor-wire fence on the border with Serbia and then Croatia. Fights with Brussels became a constant: over courts, media, universities and migration. The European Parliament started the Article 7 process against Hungary in 2018, and from 2022 the EU froze billions of euros meant for Hungary. Critics called his system corrupt and authoritarian; supporters saw a defender of Christian, national Hungary.

In February 2024 it came out that President Katalin Novák had pardoned a man convicted of helping cover up child abuse at a children's home. Novák resigned, and so did former justice minister Judit Varga. Her ex-husband turned on the government, and two years later Fidesz lost the election of 12 April 2026. Orbán conceded that night.

reigns.tagline: The insider who ended the Orbán era

paragraphs: Péter Magyar was born in Budapest in 1981 into a family of lawyers; his great-uncle Ferenc Mádl was President of Hungary. He studied law and spent years in jobs under Fidesz: at the foreign ministry, at Hungary's EU mission in Brussels, and running the state student loan agency. He was married to Judit Varga, Orbán's justice minister.

When the pardon scandal broke in February 2024 and Varga resigned, Magyar quit his state posts the same day and turned on the system he had served. Within weeks he was drawing huge crowds in Budapest. He took over a tiny party, Tisza, came second in the June 2024 European election and sat as an MEP. In 2025 he walked from Budapest to Oradea in Romania to meet Hungarians there.

On 12 April 2026, with the highest turnout since 1990, Tisza won 141 of 199 seats, a two-thirds majority. Parliament elected Magyar prime minister on 9 May. He promised to undo the Orbán system, limit prime ministers to two terms and mend relations with the EU.
